news.title: Billionaire daughter of LA Times owner is ridiculed for slamming her own father's newspaper over for Israeli tourism ad
news.text:
The daughter of LA Times owner Patrick Soon-Shiong scolded her father for allowing an Israeli tourism advert to run in the newspaper. 

Nika Soon-Shiong, a vocal pro-Palestine activist and publisher, hit out at the news outlet after learning that it's sharing a map of Israel on its website. 

The map is part of a sponsored tourism ad, and, according to Nika, it 'completely erases the occupied Palestinian territories.' 

Drop Site News, the independent publication that the 33-year-old runs, shared a lengthy post on X shaming the LA Times for running the map. 

'The sponsored content, labeled "Paid Program" and produced by the paper's branded content arm, LA Times Studios, is titled "Israel: Land of Creation," and paid for by the official tourism campaign of Israel's Ministry of Tourism.

'Its map shows a single, borderless Israel from the Mediterranean to the Jordan River, with no West Bank or Gaza, and appears to fold in the occupied Syrian Golan Heights,' the self-described 'non-aligned, investigative news organization' wrote. 

The publication went on to claim that although the promotion does not violate US law, it 'contradicts international law.' 

'The UN Security Council declared Israel's 1981 annexation of the Golan "null and void," and the International Court of Justice found in 2024 that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful and that states must not recognize it,' the post continued. 

Just hours before her site shared its views on her father's paper, Soon-Shiong shared a link to the advertisement page and wrote: 'WHAT ON EARTH?' 

The ad was paid for by Israel's Ministry of Tourism, according to Drop Site. 

Nika's discovery ignited a firestorm online, as many were just as outraged over the advert. 

'Shame on @latimes for running a paid #propaganda #campaign that completely erases #Palestine and the #Golan Heights,' an X user shared. 

Another posted: 'Shame on the @latimes. Silent on Genocide & participating in ethnic cleansing! Cancel my subscription!' 

'Everything is wrong with LA Times,' wrote someone else. 

Meanwhile, others appeared to make light of Nika and her outlet calling out LA Times over the ad. 

'Oh no! Not an advertisement. The horror,' a user shared. 

Another person simply suggested that Nika talk to her dad about her outrage. 

'Maybe talk to dad sometime!' a person said. 

After the advertisement was revealed, James Queally, a staff writer for the LA Times, shared that the newspaper is not behind it. 

'Just to be clear, the Los Angeles Times is not doing this,' Queally shared on X. 

'LA Times Studios -- a site company our owner runs using our branding for all kinds of ads, sponsored content and non-journalism that we have no input in -- is.' 

The journalist shared a second post to further back his statement. 

'I'm a union steward. We have tried to negotiate and questioned if Studios would follow any ethical journalism norms or guidelines for years. We are repeatedly told they are a "separate company",' Queally added. 

LA Times Studio and the LA Times are both part of the Los Angeles Media Group, which is led by Patrick, the CEO and chairman. 

His net worth is estimated at $18.4 billion, according to Bloomberg.

This is not the first time that Nika has slammed her father's company. 

Before the 2024 presidential election, she claimed that the LA Times did not endorse former Vice President Kamala Harris because 'the endorsement was an opportunity to repudiate justification for the widespread targeting of journalists and ongoing war on children.' 

In response, Patrick made it clear that Nika is not at all affiliated with his company. 

'Nika speaks in her own personal capacity regarding her opinion, as every community member has the right to do,' he said. 

'She does not have any role at the L.A. Times, nor does she participate in any decision or discussion with the editorial board, as has been made clear many times.'

The Daily Mail contacted Nika and Patrick Soon-Shiong for comment.
news.summary: Nika Soon-Shiong, the daughter of LA Times executive Patrick Soon-Shiong, slammed the paper for sharing an Israeli tourism advert.
news.author: Editor,Emma Richter

news.title: Conservative says 'narrowing' divide spells doom for GOP in major red state
news.text:
President Donald Trump relied on the support of white evangelical voters to win both of his presidential elections, in 2016 and 2024 — but a conservative writer argued on Sunday that he and his fellow Republicans may be gradually losing these same religious voters.

After describing the surprising strength of Democratic nominee James Talarico compared to Republican candidate Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate election, The New York Times' David French wrote that "to understand the religious dynamics of the Texas race, it’s important to absorb the true depths of the “God gap” in American politics. That gap isn’t just about white evangelicals (although it certainly is partly about them), and it’s one of the Democrats’ chief obstacles to obtaining a durable political majority."

French continued, "Any discussion of the God gap does have to begin with white evangelicals. Their numbers are vast (far more than twice as large as Black Protestants, the most loyal religious Democratic voters), and they vote in lock step. In 2024, white evangelicals voted for Trump by a 65-point margin, 82 percent to 17 percent. Trump lost all other voters by 18 points, 58 percent to 40 percent."

Although religious groups voted more heavily Republican in 2024 than in previous elections, French speculated that this may have had less to do with a permanent shift in party allegiances than in the possibility that "people of faith may not be lost to Democrats forever so much as they’re punishing Democrats — warning with their votes against the secularization and social radicalization of the far left." To support this hypothesis, he noted that President Joe Biden outperformed Vice President Kamala Harris considerably among these groups between 2020 and 2024.

French is not alone in noting that the Christian right is losing political clout and that religious voters may swing toward the Democrats. Last month, The Bulwark's Joe Perticone wrote that, ever since national abortion rights were overturned in the 2022 Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson, Christian right organizations that relied on the abortion issue to galvanize voters have been struggling instead. 

"One of the major subplots in American politics over the past half-decade is evangelical Christians—the political constituency without which Trump would have never been elected president—becoming the dog that caught the car," Perticone explained. "They just haven’t had much reason to go to the polls since June 2022, when the Supreme Court overturned the legal right to an abortion in its landmark Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision."

Trump's behavior has also turned off some Christian voters. For example, John Whitehead – founder of the powerful Christian legal movement – has argued that the movement has “gone astray" in the Trump era.

news.title: Latino Men Who Powered Trump's 2024 Win Cool on Him in New Poll
news.text: Latino men who helped fuel President Donald Trump's return to the White House in the 2024 election are turning away from him ahead of November's midterm elections, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll. Hispanic and Latino voters have historically broken for Democrats, but Trump made inroads with these voters in the last election, helping propel his return to the White House in key states, especially in places like Arizona and Nevada. Democrats have worked to win back Hispanic and Latino voters in the midterms, and a key question is whether there will be a reversion back to Democrats or if the GOP gains are permanent. A reversal among Latino men could have major implications for Republicans in November, especially in competitive House districts and statewide races in Texas, Nevada and Florida. What the Poll Shows According to the NBC News/Telemundo survey, Trump's approval rating among Latino men stands at 33 percent, while 64 percent disapprove of his job performance. The poll also found Democrats hold a 24-point advantage among Latino voters on the generic congressional ballot, with 59 percent preferring Democratic control of Congress and 35 percent favoring Republicans. While Latino women remain more Democratic than Latino men, both groups now hold largely negative views of Trump. Democrats lead Republicans among Latino women by 31 points, with 62 percent favoring Democratic control of Congress and 31 percent backing Republicans. Among Latino men, Democrats hold a narrower but still significant 16-point advantage, 53 percent to 39 percent. Even among Latino men, sentiment toward Trump has deteriorated sharply. Latino men, like the broader Latino electorate, expressed significant concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement, according to the poll. The survey found broader dissatisfaction across the Latino electorate. Trump holds a 27 percent approval rating among Latino voters overall, while 69 percent disapprove of his job performance. Seventy-four percent disapprove of his handling of the economy, 78 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living and 69 percent disapprove of his handling of immigration. Economic concerns appear to be driving much of the shift. Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters, 65 percent, said Trump's policies have hurt economic conditions, while 63 percent said their household income is falling behind the cost of living. The poll found Latino voters now give Democrats a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, a reversal from 2024 when Trump held a four-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on the issue. Meanwhile, 67 percent said Trump's immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, compared with 22 percent who said the administration has taken the right approach. In NBC News' comparable 2024 survey, Democrats' current 24-point advantage among Latino voters on the generic congressional ballot is double the lead they held at a similar point in 2024, according to NBC News polling. Still, Republicans retain some of the gains they made during the Trump era. NBC News noted that GOP support among Latino voters remains higher than in polling conducted before the 2024 election cycle, even as dissatisfaction with Trump has increased. The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters from September 21 to 28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20 percent of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the White House, Hispanic Federation and Voto Latino for comment by email Sunday. Previous Polling Results In August, CNN data analyst Harry Enten highlighted polling data showing Trump’s approval slipping among Hispanic voters. He pointed to polling data from CNN and SSRS showing that the president’s approval rating among Hispanic men is -41 points despite winning them by 10 points less than two years ago when he ran against Harris. “All of that movement that you saw, that historic performance that President Trump had among Hispanic men, adios amigos. Goodbye. See you later,” he said. Enten said the shift is largely due to the economy, with data showing his approval on the economy among Hispanic men stood at -49 points, despite being more trusted by 11 points over Harris in the fall of 2024. “What we’re seeing among Hispanic men and their views of President Trump very much diving toward the negative, absolutely look like they’re going to have a massive impact on the midterm elections,” Enten said. That data is backed up by some other polls, though many pollsters do not release crosstab data for Hispanic men specifically, as that is often a small subset that may not always be statistically significant. Civiqs, which has surveyed more than 123,000 Americans since January 2025 on Trump’s approval rating, does provide such information. It found that 59 percent of Hispanic and Latino men disapproved of Trump, while 36 percent approved. Meanwhile, a UnidosUS poll also found him underwater with Latino men, finding his approval at 34 percent and disapproval at 64 percent. It surveyed 3,000 Latino registered voters from April 27 to May 14, 2026, and had a margin of error overall of ±1.8 percentage points. What Is Behind the Shift? The economy is a central reason why Trump’s approval has fallen with Hispanic and Latino voters, Matt A. Barreto, faculty director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project and Democratic Pollster to Biden’s 2020 campaign, previously told Newsweek. “Trump made wild and unrealistic promises in 2024 about lowering the cost of living, bringing down the cost of gasoline and making healthcare more affordable," he said. "Now almost two years later he has not delivered on any of his economic promises and Latinos, men in particular, are viewing election through the lens of affordability.” While Democrats do have an opportunity to win back Latino voters, there will not be an “automatic rebound,” he said. “Democrats need to convince Latinos they are fighting for them and fighting for the middle class to bring down costs," he said. "Given how bad the Latino numbers look for Trump, Democrats should take this chance to double and triple their investment in Latino outreach in the final months.” Trump was able to win over Latino men in 2024 by promising “to address concrete economic issues” affecting them, while he also “played off the tough, deliberative male patriarch,” Charles Venator-Santiago, professor of political science at the University of Connecticut, told Newsweek. Many Latino men “generally vote like Blue Dog Democrats,” and may not be gravitating toward the party’s progressive shift, he said. He pointed to Trump’s immigration policy as one sticking point that could be costing him support. “Trump’s ICE has been racially profiling Latinos [regardless of citizenship status] and persecuting Latinos," he said. "ICE has committed civil and human rights abuses that cross various lines, even for conservative Latinos.” The NBC News/Telemundo poll showed that Latino voters ranked inflation and the cost of living as their top concern, while two-thirds said Trump's immigration enforcement policies have gone too far. The shift also comes amid heightened attention to immigration enforcement, including the July shooting death of Houston construction worker Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during an ICE operation and the nonfatal shooting of Venezuelan DoorDash driver Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. What the White House Has Said In statements previously provided to Newsweek, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle wrote that November 5, 2024, was “the ultimate poll” when “nearly 80 million Americans overwhelmingly elected President Trump to deliver on his popular and commonsense agenda. “No other President in history has accomplished more for the American people than President Trump, who is working tirelessly to create jobs, cool inflation, increase housing affordability, and more. The President has already made historic progress not only in America but around the world, and this is just the beginning as his agenda continues taking effect,” Ingle said. What Happens Next Both parties are expected to intensify efforts to win over Latino voters before the 2026 midterms. Republican pollster Micah Roberts, who conducted the poll with Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo, described Latino voters as "the swingiest of swing groups" and said the shift since 2024 was "stunning." Democrats also face challenges of their own. While Latino voters are moving away from Trump, the poll found views of the Democratic Party have not significantly improved, showing that 42 percent have a negative view of it, a 4-point increase from 2024. With 72 percent of Latino voters rating their interest in the upcoming election as a 10 out of 10 and 54 percent saying their vote is intended as a signal of opposition to Trump, both parties are likely to view Latino voters, and Latino men in particular, as among the most consequential voting blocs of this year's campaign. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Hispanic and Latino voters have historically broken for Democrats, but Trump made inroads with them in the last election.
news.author: Hollie Silverman

news.title: Take Voters' Economic Concerns Seriously, Republican Senator Warns As Midterm Polling Continues To Favor Democrats.
news.text: The outcome of the midterm elections hangs in the balance and Republican candidates should heed voters' financial concerns, John Kennedy, the Republican Senator for Louisiana, said in an interview."I do think it [the midterm results] will be close. I think the biggest issue is cost-of-living," Kennedy told NBC's Kristen Welker on Sunday. "We have to tell the American people the truth. Telling them not to believe their lying checkbooks is not going to work," the Republican politician continued.The issue of daily costs has featured prominently in campaign messaging ahead of the November vote. While holding a campaign rally for Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio on Saturday, President Donald Trump warned Americans that a Democrat victory would result "in a 1929-style economic depression".The president also reiterated his promise to issue every American adult with $5,000, a policy which has been dubbed the "Trump dividend", if Republicans win in November.However, Kennedy, who called Trump his "friend" in the interview, warned that the economic picture was not looking entirely favorable for Republicans, stating that inflation had "reared its ugly head under President Trump because of the war in Iran."Inflation levels have remained higher than they were before hostilities began in February; in May the annualized inflation rate hit a three-year high of 4.2% and, although inflation has since eased, it remained elevated in August at 3.4%. Higher energy costs are largely responsible for this continuously high inflation.Kennedy echoed Trump's repeated promises that prices would come down as soon as the conflict with Iran ends but, like Trump, did not specify a timescale for a potential settlement.The Louisiana senator was also cautious in his predictions about certain key midterm races, stating that the senate race in Texas between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton was "very, very close" and effectively an "unpopularity contest".Recent polling by the New York Times in Texas, a traditionally red state, shows Talarico pulling ahead. That same polling shows that Democrat candidates are posing serious electoral challenges for House and Senate races in several other Republican-leaning states, including Alaska, Ohio and Iowa.The results of an NBC poll of Latino voters published on Sunday spelled more trouble for the Republicans and Trump, who won a record share of the Latino vote for a Republican presidential candidate in 2024. The poll showed that 69 percent of Hispanic Americans disapprove of the Trump presidency, with only 27 percent expressing approval.The poll also showed that Latinos trust the Democrats more than the Republicans on the economy by a margin of 21 percentage points, a remarkable reversal compared to 2024, when Trump had a 4-point edge over Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris on the same issue.However, the poll was not all good news for Democrats; the party now enjoys much lower net favorability ratings (-1 percent) amongst Latino voters compared to 2018 (+26 percent).Regardless, Democrat Rahm Emanuel, a White House Chief of Staff under former President Obama and Ambassador to Japan under former President Joe Biden, was much more confident in his midterm predictions when he spoke to NBC's Welker before Kennedy on Sunday."This election is a referendum on President Trump ... all the corruption and affordability issues are all com[ing] together", Emanuel said. He also stressed to Welker that Democrats had to prove they could provide real change for voters "after the election, when we win."
news.summary: Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said that telling voters to "ignore their lying checkbooks" is a poor campaign strategy for the midterms.
news.author: Raphael McMahon

news.title: WATCH: Dem senators dodge backing Kamala Harris in potential 2028 run: ‘Very messy’
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is leaving the door open to another White House bid in 2028, but Democratic senators aren’t rushing to line up behind their party’s 2024 nominee. "Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support." "I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be." HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026 "We've got a lot of people who are going to run and I think we should sort that out after the midterms," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., said. Harris returned to the campaign trail last week alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, while continuing to leave open the possibility of another White House bid. Asked in Detroit whether she would run in 2028, Harris said she had not decided and urged Democrats to focus on November, warning that "'28 won't matter" without success in 2026. "We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're gonna win back the House and the Senate." She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26." DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 "This is going to be a wide open primary, and again, that's democracy at its best," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said. "Everyone who wants to run should be able to run for office here." Another potential 2028 contender is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who represents the party’s progressive wing. Gavin Newsom is another potential 2028 contender, although he said last month that he would not run if Harris enters the race. "We should have a lot of candidates running so we have a very broad discussion about the future of this country," Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., said. news.title: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
news.text: Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations. Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living. There are clear signs his party is paying the price. A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question. Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%. That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election. Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference. The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country. The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections. Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.” “What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.” But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012. “Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said. Trump struggles Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling. His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference. Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it. Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue. Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters. A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024. Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues. “It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.” “I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added. Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family. While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies. Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough. While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S. Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans. “There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added. In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years. Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE. Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics. She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.” “They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added. Midterms fallout The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations. “In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living. “This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said. Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms. Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections. Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community. Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past. And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way. While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party. While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024. “I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.” She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her. The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38 feeling neutral about socialism. Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message. “What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26,” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.” The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

news.title: Trump Urges Ohioans to Pass Voter ID Issue, Support GOP Candidates
news.text:
VANDALIA, Ohio—Days before early voting begins in Ohio, President Donald Trump told a cheering crowd of 4,000 that they must support Republican candidates to ensure that the state continues its upward economic trend.

“We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we’ve ever had in the history of Ohio,” Trump said Oct. 3 at the Butler–Vandalia Student Activity Center—his latest stop in a campaign blitz to support Republican candidates.

He also told Ohio supporters to vote for Issue 3, which would enshrine the state’s current voter-ID requirement in the state constitution.

Trump said Republican policies attract businesses, including Bayer, which just announced plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical center in Columbus.

Ohio was named America’s best state for business this year—the first time the state earned that honor in CNBC’s annual rankings.

He also teased the audience with the possibility of locating the newly created U.S. National Space Academy in Ohio. “If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this,” he said, noting that the state was home to the Wright Brothers, who pioneered powered flight.

Trump declared that Ohio is “booming” because of tariffs that he imposed. Virtually all U.S. states are thriving, he said, noting reduced crime rates thanks to halting illegal border crossings and deporting illegal immigrants who have criminal records.

Trump also pointed to stock-market record highs, higher 401(k) balances, record income levels, manufacturing job gains, and large private investment in U.S. factories.

The president added that his policies put more money in Americans’ pockets through tax cuts and by eliminating taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security income. And he repeated his call for $5,000 dividends to be paid to adult U.S. citizens if Republicans keep the House and Senate.

Trump’s Ohio visit came exactly a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, following rallies in Texas, Oklahoma, and Alabama; other stops are planned.

Nearing the midpoint of his second and final term as president, Trump framed the midterm election as a chance to defeat “radical left” Democrats, including some who may be aligned with socialist or communist policies. Voter registration in Ohio closes on Oct. 5; early in-person voting begins on Oct. 6.

As the Ohio rallygoers repeatedly sprang to their feet, pumping fists, whistling, cheering, and stomping on the bleachers, Trump commended the crowd for its exuberant support. “I think they have more spirit here than at the Ohio State University’s football game,” he said.

The president urged attendees to translate that enthusiasm into votes. “Just get out and vote. If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” the president said.

He also said they should pass the constitutional amendment requiring voters to present ID cards. “I love that,” he said, calling the measure “your chance to stop Democrat cheaters, fraudsters, and defend Ohio elections for your children and for your grandchildren.”

“So do not miss this chance. Vote yes on issue three to require voter ID,” Trump said.

Trump’s rally was intended to boost the Republican slate, particularly gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio)—both of whom face tight races against Democrats, according to recent polling.

Ramaswamy is running against former Ohio health director Dr. Amy Acton. The incumbent, Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, cannot run again because of term limits.

Husted was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance when the latter joined the Trump administration.

Although Husted is new to Capitol Hill, he formerly served as Ohio’s lieutenant governor and secretary of state. Trump said that Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.), the majority leader, told him that Husted quickly became one of the most respected members of the U.S. Senate.

Husted’s opponent is former longtime Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio)—whom Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) unseated in 2024.

Speaking about the upcoming midterms, Trump dismissed the accuracy of polls showing tight races for GOP candidates.

“Nobody counted on the fact that Trump was going to go out and campaign for all these people—because when I do, we win,” he said.

Although the RealClearPolitics average of opinion polls shows the president has a low approval rating of 38.2 percent, rallygoers and politicos who spoke to The Epoch Times said the president remains popular in Ohio. He won the state by 11 percentage points in the 2024 election against then-Vice President Kamala Harris, a Democrat.

Asked about support for Trump reportedly waning, rally attendee Matthew Jackson of Columbus said, “I haven’t seen that,” adding, “I’ve never seen this kind of excitement.”

Jackson, a firefighter and Navy veteran running for the Ohio House, said GOP grassroots-building efforts noticeably ramped up in August with door-knocking and texting campaigns. He thinks that could have whipped up the base that showed up Saturday.

Although dozens of protesters gathered outside the venue, inside “everyone was excited and welcoming,” Jackson said.

Jacob Sargent, the 27-year-old chairman of the Ohio Young Republicans, said he was unconcerned about recent unfavorable polling because he has often seen polls “underrepresenting Republicans” during his four years of campaign work.

Frequent Trump rally attendee Brenda White, wearing a giant hat with Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan, cited a reason why it’s hard to accurately gauge support for Trump.

“People are still afraid to say that they’re Trump fans, and I don’t know why—because he’s the greatest president in my lifetime,” the 66-year-old Lorain woman said. “He truly is.”

Sargent further explained why he’s confident Republicans will do better than expected in the midterms.

While visiting all 88 counties in the state, he has seen a pattern: Democrats won elections in 2006 on the strength of support from Ohio’s Appalachian and working-class blocs.

“And that doesn’t exist anymore,” Sargent said. “The Democrats have completely abandoned that base, and they’re not going to be able to make up those numbers.”

Messaging from Acton and other Democrats has focused largely on affordability—an issue that is “absolutely the bread-and-butter of the American psyche when they go to the polls.”

But Sargent said conditions now are much better than they were under President Joe Biden in 2020–2024.

Many costs have dropped or stabilized, he said, pointing out that Ramaswamy was instrumental in pushing lawmakers to adopt the 90-day state gasoline tax rollback now in effect.

“We’re seeing it getting better,” Sargent said, “and we have full faith and trust in our president and the Republican Party to continue to deliver those wins across the nation.”

The state boasts the largest federation of young Republicans in America, he said, with 1,300 members in 48 counties. Many were in attendance at the rally and led some of the chanting.

“We’re fired up,” Sargent said. “We’re ready for this election.”

news.text:
For years, the goblin architects of globo-homo race communism have labored tirelessly behind the scenes, in the shadows where they prefer to operate, to push through a so-called “global pandemic treaty” that would standardize the international response to the impending, much-hyped (probably man-made) pandemic, thereby subverting any national sovereignty that would allow room for individualized decision-making by nation-states.

Related: WHO Accuses Anti-Vaxxers of 'Anti-Science Aggression,' Calls Them 'Killing Force'

In her speech announcing American opposition to the treaty, CDC Director Erica Schwartz also promoted the banning, on a national basis, of the gain-of-function research that almost certainly sparked the COVID-19 pandemic.

Via The Hill (emphasis added):

news.title: Before you ask us to trust again
news.text:
When the Walter Reed scandal erupted in 2007, the officers under fire were more than names in a newspaper to me. I knew many of them. I saw their frustration and outrage as they scrambled to address failures some were only then discovering.

My wife, Gracie, and I were at Walter Reed frequently. A bilateral amputee herself, she had been invited to sing and spend time with wounded warriors, particularly women returning from Iraq and Afghanistan with amputations. The military was struggling to care for troops with devastating injuries, many caused by improvised explosive devices.

We cannot turn the page simply because the people responsible do not want us to read it.

Knowing people working there helped me understand the strain. Knowing more wounded were coming helped me understand why the failures could not wait.

The Washington Post exposed serious problems in outpatient conditions and care, including mold, vermin, bureaucratic delays, and wounded soldiers falling through administrative cracks. The reporting was painful for people I knew. It was also necessary.

I discussed the scandal with my father, a retired Navy captain. The military, he explained, survives by folding painful lessons into its policies, procedures, and institutional memory so others do not have to learn them at the same cost.

That is what an after-action review is for: What happened? Why did it happen? What changes now?

The lesson must outlive the embarrassment.

When our leaders and the media lie, conceal, or confidently tell us something that later proves false, they do the heavy lifting for our enemies. How do we defend the country together when we cannot trust the people describing the danger?

Consider the assurances about President Biden’s capacity. In February 2024, press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre said, “He is sharp. He is on top of things.” In March, MSNBC’s Joe Scarborough went much further, calling the sitting president “the best Biden ever” intellectually and analytically.

Then came the June debate and Biden’s withdrawal from the race in July.

The debate did not establish a medical diagnosis. It did demand an explanation from people who had spent months assuring the public that concerns about Biden’s capacity were misplaced.

In May 2025, Scarborough finally said, “I was obviously wrong.” He explained that his confidence came from extended personal encounters with Biden. Then he added that he was not sure what lesson to take from the episode.

That’s precisely the problem.

What evidence did he discount? What did he see that persuaded him? What did others see that contradicted it? What will he do differently next time?

RELATED: Gavin Newsom invoked Nietzsche. I thought of ‘Blazing Saddles.’

 Sean Rayford/Getty Images

Those questions belong not only to Scarborough but to every politician, aide, reporter, editor, broadcaster, and institution that gave the public confident assurances. An after-action review cannot end with “I was wrong” any more than it can end with “I meant well.”

The next people relying on you need to know what changed.

The border demands the same accounting. In September 2022, Vice President Kamala Harris said, “The border is secure.” In October 2023, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas testified that more than 600,000 known “gotaways” had evaded apprehension during that fiscal year.

What did “secure” mean? More important, what evidence would have caused the administration to abandon that description sooner?

An honest accounting must distinguish between what officials got wrong and what they knowingly concealed. That requires records, testimony, names, timelines, and decisions. Citizens should not have to settle for whichever explanation best protects a party, an administration, or a network.

We may expect politicians to lie. That does not excuse them. Nor does it relieve journalists of the obligation to test what politicians say rather than repeat it.

Over 40 years of caregiving, I have had plenty of doctors get things wrong. I understand the reluctance to offer a mea culpa. But I take their advice home and live with the consequences. If we are going to continue together, I need to know how the next decision will be better.

RELATED: The fourth bus of the Apocalypse

 Miguel Perfectti/Getty Images

That was the obligation at Walter Reed. The next wounded soldier needed the previous failure corrected whether anyone responsible felt sorry or not.

“Mistakes were made” leaves the authors conveniently absent. “Turn the page” asks the public to move on while the questions remain unanswered.

We cannot turn the page simply because the people responsible do not want us to read it.

Our enemies benefit from failures we refuse to examine. If those responsible will not come clean, voters should elect people willing to use lawful investigations, public hearings, compelled testimony, and the release of records to establish what happened. Where evidence establishes crimes, pursue prosecution.

But a hearing cannot become the place where accountability goes to die.

The Constitution provides authority. The law provides tools. Voters must supply people willing to use them.

This election, ask candidates whose records they will demand, which decisions they will examine, and whether their own allies will have to answer questions under oath. Anyone can promise to investigate an opponent. The test comes when the evidence reaches a friend.

I owe my preferred candidates and broadcasters that same scrutiny. Excusing them would preserve the very failure I want corrected.

We can disagree on policy and still defend this country shoulder to shoulder. But we cannot make truth optional. Calls for unity ring hollow when the people asking for trust refuse to account for how they broke it.

Our children will inherit whatever we excuse.

news.title: How George Clooney's Possible 2028 Dem President Picks Are Faring
news.text: Actor George Clooney has identified three Democrats he is watching ahead of the 2028 presidential election, but the actor and prominent Democratic fundraiser says he plans to wait until after November's midterm elections before endorsing anyone. That means the November 3 elections could provide an early political test for two of the three figures he singled out: Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, both of whom are seeking reelection this year. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear, meanwhile, is not up for election this November. Speaking at The Future of Creativity event in Venice in September, Clooney said, "I think we're all very excited by this young senator from Georgia, Jon Ossoff. I am 65 years old, and I think that we need some young voices that are coming up with new ideas and some new thoughts." He also said he liked Pritzker and Beshear, while making clear that he had not yet settled on a candidate. Newsweek has contacted representatives for Clooney, Ossoff, Pritzker and Beshear for comment. The remarks are notable because of Clooney's high-profile intervention in the 2024 presidential election. In a New York Times opinion essay in July 2024, he called on President Joe Biden to end his reelection campaign after Biden's poor debate performance against Donald Trump. Biden withdrew later that month and endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris, who became the Democratic nominee before losing to Trump. For now, however, early polling suggests none of Clooney's three prospective choices is the clear favorite for the Democratic nomination. The RealClearPolling national average, covering polls from July 19 through September 28, has Harris at 26.3 percent, California Governor Gavin Newsom at 14.3 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 12.6 percent, and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 10 percent. Ossoff follows at 8.8 percent, while Beshear is at 4 percent and Pritzker at 3.2 percent. In a September 26-28 Harvard-Harris poll, for example, Ossoff registered 6 percent and Pritzker 5 percent, while Harris had 38 percent. An Echelon Insights poll conducted September 17-21 put Ossoff at 8 percent and both Beshear and Pritzker at 2 percent. A July Emerson poll painted a different picture, giving Ossoff 13 percent and Beshear 7 percent. Ossoff Faces an Immediate Test Of Clooney's three names, Ossoff currently has the strongest standing in national presidential polling and faces perhaps the most consequential test next month. The Georgia Democrat, elected to the Senate in a January 2021 runoff, is seeking another term against Republican Rep. Mike Collins on November 3. Ossoff's first Senate victory came by a narrow margin over Republican David Perdue. The RealClearPolling average has Ossoff at 51.1 percent to Collins' 43.1 percent, an eight-point advantage. Its listed September polls have all shown Ossoff ahead, although by margins ranging from four to 10 percentage points. A September Big Data Poll survey of 678 likely Georgia voters found Ossoff leading Collins by 55 percent to 45 percent, an 11-point margin. The poll was conducted September 21-23. For Ossoff, a second consecutive victory could also strengthen his standing in conversations about the Democratic Party's future. Clooney's own remarks suggest Ossoff's age is part of his appeal. At 39, Ossoff represents a younger generation of elected Democrats at a time when the party continues to debate generational change following the 2024 election. As of October 4, Ocasio-Cortez leads the Polymarket odds for the 2028 Democratic nomination at about 17 percent, followed by Newsom at 16 percent and Ossoff at 15 percent. Harris stands at 7 percent, Shapiro at 6 percent, Buttigieg at 5 percent, Beshear at 3 percent, and Pritzker at about 1 percent. Prediction-market prices reflect traders’ expectations rather than public opinion. An August Emerson College survey has Ossoff leading Vice President JD Vance 49 percent to 44 percent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio 47 percent to 44 percent in hypothetical 2028 matchups. Such polling this far ahead of an election is highly provisional and measures voter preferences under hypothetical candidate fields rather than forecasting an eventual result. Pritzker Seeks Another Term Pritzker also faces voters on November 3 as the Illinois Democrat seeks another term as governor. Unlike Ossoff, however, there is relatively little recent public polling of his state race. The RealClearPolling page for a Pritzker matchup against Republican Darren Bailey lists a November 2025 Victory Research survey of 1,200 likely voters that gave Pritzker a 54-34 percent advantage. Pritzker defeated Bailey in their 2022 contest by double digits. His potential presidential standing is more modest. The current RealClearPolling national average puts him at 3.2 percent for the 2028 Democratic nomination. Recent individual results include 5 percent in the late-September Harvard-Harris poll and 2 percent in September's Echelon Insights survey. Those numbers place him well behind the leading names currently being tested, but the Democratic field remains wide open. Beshear Polling in the Low Single Digits Beshear, a two-term Democratic governor in Republican-leaning Kentucky, is Clooney's third name. Unlike Ossoff and Pritzker, Beshear does not face voters in the 2026 midterm elections. His current gubernatorial term followed his reelection in 2023. In national polling of a potential 2028 Democratic field, Beshear generally remains in the low single digits. The RealClearPolling average has him at 4 percent, ahead of Pritzker but behind Ossoff and several other potential contenders. The July Emerson survey put him at 7 percent, while Big Data Poll had him at 4 percent in September. Echelon Insights placed him at 2 percent later that month. Beshear previously told Newsweek that he believes the next president should be a Democratic governor, arguing that governors have the executive experience needed for the White House. A Race That Has Barely Begun The polling picture offers an important caveat to Clooney's shortlist. That volatility makes the early numbers better viewed as snapshots of name recognition and current voter preference than reliable predictions of a presidential contest still two years away. Clooney himself has left his options open. He said in September that he would not endorse anyone until after the midterms, while ruling out a run of his own. For Ossoff and Pritzker, November 3 will provide something more concrete than hypothetical presidential polling: a test at the ballot box before Clooney and other Democratic donors and voters begin making firmer judgments about the party's 2028 field. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon and Cristina Diciu.
news.summary: Clooney is watching Ossoff, Pritzker and Beshear as possible 2028 Democratic contenders. Here’s how his three picks are faring.

news.title: Why Ken Paxton could lose a Texas GOP Senate seat to James Talarico
news.text:
Tamara Berger is miffed at the backhanded praise President Donald Trump gave Texas state Attorney General Ken Paxton at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

"Let me tell you, it's true, he may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best looking guy I've ever seen," Trump told a laughing audience at the American Airlines Center on Sept. 9 about the Republican Senate nominee.

"But you know what he is? He's the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator."

The president's remarks may have rubbed some conservative voters the wrong way, but they are an acknowledgement of how uniquely burdened Paxton is in the face of past bribery allegations and marital drama — even as Republicans are counting on the Texas attorney general to hold on to the seat many in the GOP consider a must-win.

Berger, 56, who lives in Seguin, Texas, said she was "disgusted" by Trump's presentation, even if he was joking, and called Paxton an "American through and through."

Asked what advice she would give Paxton to win over voters on the fence, Berger, who voted for Trump three times responded, "Give me a break. Nobody is perfect."

"I don't agree with his private life, but I also don't know all the details," she added. "There's always two sides to a story, and that's not my place to judge. We've all had personal grievances. So has Biden. So has (Bill) Clinton. So has pretty much every other politician."

Her remarks highlight the reason Paxton is vulnerable to an upset by Democrat James Talarico: the Republican is viewed favorably by 43% of likely voters and unfavorably by 55%, according to a late September poll from Texas Southern University.

Polls also show Paxton with little appeal to some pivotal segments of the electorate. The Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin found in August that just 29% of suburban voters viewed Paxton favorably, versus 54% who viewed him unfavorably. The same survey found 43% of Texas suburbanites looked at Talarico in a favorable light compared with 34% who viewed him unfavorably.

The result: A state Trump carried by 14 percentage points in 2024 is surprisingly competitive. Multiple surveys show a tight race, with some finding Talarico up by as much as 6 percentage points.

"Republicans have arrived at this really problematic situation where they have a candidate that we know much of the professional Republican class thought was vulnerable and would be not the best candidate to have at the top of the ballot," said James Henson, executive director of the Texas Politics Project, which conducts public opinion polling. "But that is counterbalanced by a Republican base that in the primaries just seemed determined to vote for him and and to nominate him."

Majority of Texans say Paxton isn't honest or trustworthy: poll

Trump helped Paxton defeat Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary this summer, despite warnings from some GOP strategists that tossing out the four-term senator in favor of someone less popular would be risky in an-already difficult year for Republicans.

During the GOP primary, for instance, a Republican operative close to the Cornyn campaign told USA TODAY that Senate leaders and former Trump campaign officials were pressuring the president to oppose Paxton, in light of his 2023 impeachment on bribery charges by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives.

Paxton was accused of using his power as state attorney general to benefit a real estate developer who helped remodel his home and who employed a woman with whom Paxton allegedly had an affair. The attorney general has consistently denied the bribe charges, and the state Senate acquitted him after a two-week trial.

In 2025 his wife, Angela Paxton, a state legislator, announced on X the two were getting a divorce based on "biblical grounds" after being married almost four decades. Other embarrassing episodes include being forced to return another lawyer's $1,000 pen that he plucked at a Texas courthouse in 2013.

The Paxton campaign declined repeated requests for comment, but public polls show those controversies have seeped into the minds of most voters.

When asked how well the phrase "honest and trustworthy" describes Paxton, just one-third of voters said very to somewhat well, a survey conducted by the Texas Politics Project in August found. More than half of respondents, however, said the opposite, including 29% of Republicans and 44% of independents who said "not at all."

Henson said the startling part of the poll is that only a quarter of Republican voters selected "very well" when asked about Paxton's honesty and trustworthiness.

"Ideally, your marquee candidate at the top of the ballot is going to be doing significantly better than that," he said.

The Paxton campaign, he said, faces three risks: Republicans who vote for Talarico or a third-party candidate, those who stay home and others who leave their ballot blank for Senate.

That, combined with a sinking approval rating for Trump, has put a seat that Cornyn won four times by comfortable margins in the "toss-up" column, according to forecasters such as the non-partisan Cook Political Report.

'Foolish': Republicans weigh options as Cornyn keeps swinging

The Talarico campaign has applied its own pressure to the sore spots in the GOP coalition, such as by highlighting how it hired a longtime Cornyn staffer and appealing to historically conservative factions. Speaking at a Sept. 28 forum hosted by the U.S. Hispanic Business Council in Fort Worth, Texas, Talarico said farmers and ranchers have been "screwed over" by those in office.

Republican Glen Whitley, a retired state judge, is supporting the political newcomer over Paxton. He said in an interview that corruption allegations have hounded Paxton for years, and Texans are fed up.

"Just at every turn people catch him doing things basically for himself instead of serving the public," Whitley told USA TODAY. "That's just not something that people appreciate of an elected official."

Among GOP voters who identify as "strong Republicans" Paxton holds a 74% approval, the Texas Politics Project survey shows. But that drops to around 40% among those who self-described as "not very strong" or as "lean Republican," the poll finds.

Republicans have also failed to reconcile since the primary battle, typified by Cornyn telling CNN on Sept. 25 that he has no plans to support Paxton's campaign, "for all the reasons we pointed out in the primary."

The senator has also called his GOP rival "lazy" and a "poor campaigner."

Republican Brenda Foster, 83, supported Cornyn in the primary, which saw the senator and allies spend $90 million criticizing Paxton, often on personal grounds. She admitted the attorney general is "coming with too much baggage," but the Lubbock, Texas, native still plans to pull the lever for the GOP nominee.

"You only have two choices, and if you're going to vote, I think you'd be foolish to vote for Talarico," Foster, a retired school teacher, said.

"My fear is that people will stay at home because they somehow can't support Paxton, and they don't see it the same way I do," she added. "I see it as a clear choice, but I do not think that some will necessarily vote for Paxton."

Scott Teer, 67, a facilities manager in Richardson, Texas, said he isn't a fan of Paxton's "moral character" but that ties to Trump, support for border security and opposition to the Biden administration are persuasive enough.

"I agree with him 90% of the time," he said.

Others who spoke with the USA TODAY Network, such as Dylan Barron, 19, a student at the University of Texas at El Paso, emphasized how the Senate race represents an opportunity to hold on to Texas' conservative roots.

"I'm a Republican," he said. "I'm not really a fan of the Democrats."

David de la Fuente, a senior analyst at Third Way, a Democratic think tank, said going into the final stretch of the midterms Paxton is considered the "single weakest Senate nominee" this year, comparing him unfavorably to Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

"Almost a decade ago, (Democrat) Beto O'Rourke came within three points of Ted Cruz, just because (Cruz) is not the most likable dude," he said. "But, to our knowledge, Cruz has never cheated on his wife, has not committed any big crimes and O'Rourke still got within three points of him in a good Democratic cycle."

Public polling by the Texas Politics Project on the eve of the 2018 midterms showed roughly 50% of suburban voters held a favorable view of Cruz versus 40% with an unfavorable one.

Paxton trashes convention, touts personal uplift

Paxton, a staunch Trump supporter, has tried to moderate his image by investigating controversial data centers and showcasing a softer side by talking about past health struggles.

During the U.S. Hispanic Business Council in Fort Worth, Texas, he recounted a childhood eye injury that partially impaired his vision. He criticized the current healthcare system as inadequate before touting a plan that he says will include a $25,000 tax deduction for medical expenses and another $25,000 per dependent.

"When I was a child, poor medical care permanently damaged my eye," Paxton said in a Sept. 28 post on X. "It taught me how important quality, affordable healthcare is for families."

Republicans are spending millions attacking Talarico, a 37-year-old state legislator and Presbyterian seminary student, as too liberal or not masculine enough.

"This race is about defending Texas and our country," Paxton said during a Sept. 30 rally in El Paso. "It is also about safeguarding our faith and our way of life. I've never seen someone so willing to weaponize faith to sell a radical agenda."

Whitley, the retired judge, said relying on culture war attacks and Trump's popularity may not work out either, given the president's approval rating has sunk to a career low of 31% in the latest Associated Press-NORC polling released Oct. 1.

In Texas, the president's job approval is 43%, with a 51% disapproval, according to the Texas Politics Project survey. In a Sept. 30 report, The New York Times obtained an audio recording of Paxton saying that Trump's midterm convention didn't deliver the boost many GOP officials had promised.

"So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers," he said. "Everybody’s numbers dropped."

Nick Maddux, a senior adviser to Paxton, described the report to USA TODAY as "manipulated nonsense" in a statement, but did not address his candidate's comments. Instead he said the attorney general, "looks forward to closing strong" alongside Trump, including an Oct. 1 stop by the president at a manufacturing plant in Denton, Texas.

Trump still receives a thumbs-up from the vast majority of Texas Republicans, who give him an 83% job approval rating, according to the Politics Project survey. But that is noticeably down from the 92% who approved of his performance in February 2025.

Terrie Kieper, an independent who lives in Garland, Texas, voted for the president in 2016. But she said the Republican Party has been turned into a "yes men" party for Trump, voting for Biden in 2020 and former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

The former financial analyst is eager to cast a ballot for Gov. Greg Abbott and other Republicans on the ballot this year, but she remains torn about supporting either of the "dirty socks" running for Senate.

"I would hate myself to give Paxton my vote because I don't trust him at all," Kieper, 57, said in an interview. "I trust him about as far as I can throw the White House, with or without a ballroom."

Contributing: Natassia Paloma, Adam Powell

news.title: Jerome Powell off the hook for the ‘Palace of Versailles’ renovation — but he’s still guilty of being a lousy Fed Chair
news.text:
Jerome Powell was cleared of criminal wrongdoing in the Fed’s $2.5 billion “Palace of Versailles” headquarters fiasco — but what about the rest of his screwups as head of the nation’s central bank? 

I’m not saying that Powell’s dismal, eight-plus year tenure as Fed chair was criminal in a legal sense, but it was hardly one of success. In fact, it has cost the American people dearly and still does.

It’s a shame all of that was overshadowed by the faux charge over whether he lied to Congress about the cost overruns for the Fed’s HQ renovation, propelled by President Trump’s often irrational disdain for Powell refusing to cut rates. IMHO, Powell should have been ousted for incompetence, plain and simple.

 Again, I’m not taking Trump’s side in the long-running soap opera to fire Powell while the president obsessed about less significant lower short-term rates (it’s the rate on the 10-year Treasury that pegs consumer borrowing that counts and is controlled by the markets). 

That showdown was one of the few bright spots of Powell’s tenure as chair: Even he knew that cutting Fed Funds when the economy was booming would upend confidence in the Fed, stoke already sticky inflation and worsen the price impact of Trump’s tariffs and the Iran conflict.

But that doesn’t come close to exempting Powell from being a bad Fed chair, whether it’s over his opulent new office space or his poor record fighting inflation.

If you read about his official exoneration from criminal liability over the BS that he lied to Congress, it only underscores his ineptitude. Don’t let his exculpation from actual crime detract from the fact that this guy can’t handle a simple reconstruction effort, much less heading the most important central bank in the world.

Kudos to my colleague, The Post’s James Franey, for breaking the story that started the entire controversy. Back in April 2025, he reported that the HQ redo was initially estimated to cost around $1.9 billion when it was first envisioned back in 2021 but was expected to balloon upwards to $2.5 billion by the time it’s finished in 2027.

Know how to add

The Fed wouldn’t be the first agency in DC guilty of serious cost overruns. But it is the nation’s central bank. The folks running it are supposed to give confidence to the world that the US dollar is stable and should remain the reserve currency. They control the money supply and a $32 trillion economy, so they should know how to add.

Worse is what they spent this money on. As Franey reported, central bankers were eyeing amenities that include “rooftop garden terraces, skylights, ornate water features and a new elevator system that allows board members to be dropped off directly in their VIP dining suite.”

What ever happened to government workers doing their jobs from cubicles?

As I mentioned, the entire mess was never criminal as Trump tried to argue in his attempts to get Powell out of the way, and as the Fed’s inspector general last week confirmed. Cost overruns are as reliable in DC as cherry blossoms in springtime.

But it was a tell that Powell wasn’t up for the job. Recall, this is a Fed chair who seemed to relish in printing money when his job No. 1 is price stability.

Initial criticism

Powell was appointed by Trump in 2018 during the president’s first term in 2018. A year later, Trump launched an initial round of Powell bashing that was actually successful, getting him to back off necessary rate hikes while the economy was humming. When COVID shut down the economy, Powell’s response was to print money ad nauseam. He didn’t stop until way after the pandemic ebbed and people were largely back at work.

The result: inflation that was far from transitory, peaking above 9% in June 2022 despite Powell’s public statements, forcing him to eventually raise rates. The rate of inflation soon fell, but prices remained elevated (even today), a key reason why Joe Biden had little shot at re-election (aside from his dismal debate performance), and then-VP Kamala Harris couldn’t make the case she was a suitable steward of the economy.

How did Powell miss the nontransitory nature of inflation? Maybe it’s the same reason he missed the cost overruns happening at this new HQ: He doesn’t spend enough time on what really matters at the Federal Reserve. Case in point: In 2022, the Fed developed a “Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Strategic Plan” to reflect the Federal Reserve Board’s “strategic initiative on diversity, equity and inclusion, which is a shared responsibility of all Board employees.”

Not exactly a great strategy to help the Fed keep inflation in check, or figure out the true cost of rooftop garden terraces and ornate water features at its new HQ.
news.summary: Jerome Powell was cleared of criminal wrongdoing in the Fed’s $2.5 billion “Palace of Versailles” headquarters fiasco — but what about the rest of his screwups as head of the nation’s central bank?

news.title: Michael Goodwin: Trump faces an uphill battle to sell voters on his agenda before the midterms — here’s how he can do it
news.text:
Although he wrote and has lived his life by the “Art of the Deal,” Donald Trump faces a giant hurdle in trying to persuade voters to keep his party in control of Washington.

Over the next month, he must successfully sell the idea that his presidency has been a big success, and that he needs a Republican congress to help him finish the job.

Midterm elections commonly spell trouble for the occupant of the White House, but Trump’s challenge is far from ordinary.

With his personal popularity sagging and his party a decided underdog in swing districts and states, the president must move mountains of voters and do it quickly.

Election Day on Nov. 3 is approaching on the fast track, and the urgency is compounded because nearly all states allow some form of early voting.

Showing that he realizes his political life and legacy are on the line, the president plans to spend most of October barnstorming America, with reports saying he aims to visit at least 10 states.

The scale of the challenge is indicated by the fact that his first stops were in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama — states that are usually reliably red, but are not yet secured this year.

The extended tour is unusual, but Trump has little choice. With polls and betting markets predicting Dems will win majorities in both the House and Senate, the president’s final two years in office will be the stuff of nightmares unless he can engineer a stunning comeback.

Otherwise, we know what the template of failure looks like — the second half of his first term. After Dems won a House majority in 2018 and made Nancy Pelosi Speaker, she orchestrated investigations of nearly every breath the president took and every dollar he spent.

Thanks to the help of leftist partisans carrying media credentials and a corrupt deep state, she turned the Russia-gate hoax into an impeachment farce.

A similar fate would be certain to befall the president again, with Dems now largely running on a “Get Trump” platform. Under the sway of burn-it-down radicals, their agenda ranges from more impeachment to imposing sky-high taxes on families and businesses, demonizing Israel and re-opening borders to all comers.

Trump knows as much, but his schedule shows he believes voters can be persuaded that he and the GOP congress have earned the right to stay the course.

In important ways, the president has a strong case, but the success of his travels and rallies will depend on how persuasively he makes that case.

Messaging trap

With the Real Clear Politics average of polls showing he has an approval rating of just 38%, compared with 60% disapproval, he faces a steep climb.

Inflation is still driving up prices, and most Americans are giving Trump poor grades on the economy. Majorities are also tired of the war in Iran, so how the president makes his final pitch could be the deciding factor in November.

One hurdle is that he has fallen into the trap of telling people how great everything is when their day-to-day experiences, especially when it comes to rising prices, are telling them something very different.

The message that all is well was a bust when Joe Biden and Kamala Harris tried it in 2024, and it’s not working any better for Trump.

One factor is the president’s habit of premature declarations of victory, over both inflation and Iran. An alternative approach, even at this late hour, would be to acknowledge public concerns and explain why he believes he and a GOP congress will achieve widely beneficial victories.

To judge from comments he made at the White House on Thursday, the president is not yet ready to go there.

“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything” he said, according to Politico. An AP-NORC poll found just 26% approve of his handling of the economy, with a mere 17% happy with how he has managed the cost of living.

More alarming, a whopping 65% told pollsters White House policies are contributing to price hikes on everyday goods.

Countering that sentiment is difficult, but it is essential to highlight economic success stories. The Census Bureau reports that median household income is the highest on record at $87,400.

Working class key

Similarly, The Wall Street Journal reports that the 4.2% unemployment rate is “at a historically low level that indicates the labor market remains generally healthy.”

Stock markets have soared as many businesses have reported record earnings, with the S&P 500 gaining 37% since Trump’s reelection.

Weaving these accomplishments together while also recognizing that many families feel left out is difficult, but the effort is essential. Charting when and why the tide will change and lift all boats would give voters concrete reasons to stick with the team in place.

Railing against the polls as being biased won’t work, nor will boasts that the nation is living in a golden age of peace and prosperity.

Ditto for promoting grand Washington construction projects, whether it be an expanded White House ballroom or an Arch of Triumph armed with snipers and drones.

They are not likely to win over disillusioned voters, especially those troubled by Trump family members taking financial advantage of the presidency.

As for Iran, many Americans no doubt forget his patient efforts to negotiate a treaty for the mullahs to voluntarily give up their nuclear weapons project.

The regime’s refusal to even consider the idea led to the US and Israeli attacks that, I continue to believe, were fully justified.

Also absent so far in the president’s election-year pitch is the working-class appeal that lifted him to a smashing victory over Harris two years ago.

Those appeals were the heart of his campaign, just as they were in his shocking upset win over Hillary Clinton in 2016.

Two October events in the ’24 race still stand out as hilarious and wildly effective. In the first, Trump spent 30 minutes working in a McDonald’s outside Philadelphia. He wore a store apron over his suit and learned how to prepare french fries and handed bags of them to cars from a drive-through window.

Ten days later, in Green Bay, Wis., he got off his plane and climbed into the passenger seat of a large garbage truck that featured his name.

Sporting a yellow and orange safety vest over a white shirt, Trump asked reporters, “How do you like my garbage truck?”

It came just one day after Biden had said something to the effect that all Trump supporters were garbage.

Point made!

Both events were hailed because they were funny, as well as consistent with his pitch to working-class Americans.

It’s not a coincidence that he carried both Wisconsin and Pennsylvania that November, along with five other swing states.

His challenge now is to help his party do it all again.
news.summary: Midterm elections commonly spell trouble for the occupant of the White House, but President Trump’s challenge is far from ordinary.
