news.title: Becerra’s battles are against Trump, who’s not on ballot
news.text:
Xavier Becerra walked into CNN’s Burbank studio Wednesday night as the heavy favorite to be California’s next governor. He walked out the same way. But anyone expecting the debate to demonstrate why the state’s former attorney general and Biden Cabinet secretary holds such a commanding lead in the race was disappointed.

For 60 minutes, the Democratic Party nominee, and Steve Hilton, his Republican challenger, seemingly fought to a draw in a race in which Becerra has been cruising.

Becerra’s campaign has kept him on a short leash for months, rationing public appearances and agreeing to exactly one general-election debate. Hilton opened the night’s stage by welcoming him to the campaign and thanking CNN “for bringing Xavier out of hiding.”

Given that the expectations for the well-seasoned but lackluster former state attorney general and Biden administration Health and Human Services secretary were low, Becerra cleared them comfortably. Becerra was sharper, quicker, and more articulate than many observers expected, and at times genuinely combative.

One word, 40 times

Becerra’s game plan was simple and predictable. By CNN’s count he said Donald Trump’s name at least 40 times in an hour – and wasn’t shy about tying Hilton to the president.

“He’s your supporter – you chased his endorsement,” Becerra asserted.

Asked about Hilton’s plan to eliminate state income taxes for middle-class Californians, Becerra answered: “You’re going to end up with Trump results if you follow Steve Hilton’s plans.”

Asked about artificial intelligence, Becerra went to the same well: “If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response by Steve Hilton.”

On oil drilling, on homelessness, on immigration, on housing, the answer kept circling back to a man who is dominating national political headlines but has rarely campaigned in California and will not be on the California ballot in November.

It’s a predictable tactic in a state where the president is deeply unpopular, but it’s not a governing agenda and some 20 minutes into the debate, Hilton said what many viewers may have been thinking.

“All you ever say is Trump, Trump, Trump, and that’s nothing but an insult to every Californian,” the former Fox News host remarked.

The night’s sharpest contrast came on the issue of employment.

“Who’s been in charge when all those jobs have gone?” Hilton asked, referring to the state’s flagging film industry.

“Donald Trump,” Becerra replied.

“The Democrats,” Hilton shot back.

Both men were sticking to their scripts. Becerra wants voters thinking about Washington. Hilton wants them thinking about Sacramento, where Democrats have held every lever of power for 16 years.

The fourth man on the stage

Trump wasn’t the only absent figure who loomed large in the Burbank studio. Gavin Newsom, term-limited and leaving office in January – and presumably running for president in 2028 – also figured prominently. Becerra spent the night running against the man in the White House while Hilton spent it running against the man in the governor’s office – and against the record Becerra is asking voters to extend.

That’s an awkward spot for Becerra. He was attorney general for the first two years of Newsom’s tenure, and much of what Hilton pressed him on, from affordability and fraud to billions spent vainly on homelessness, is a record the two Democrats share. Every time Becerra pointed to Washington, Hilton pointed back to Sacramento and the governor whose job Becerra wants. Becerra was happy to keep the fight on Trump. He showed little appetite for a fight over Newsom’s record.

Hilton’s hits

When Becerra attacked Hilton’s proposed tax cuts with the old saw that the “definition of insanity” was doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results, Hilton snapped back: “Like voting Democrat.”

It was an easy opening, and Becerra handed it to him. Hilton then used Becerra’s “insanity” line against him repeatedly. On the issue of whether California has over-regulated everything from business regulations to housing construction, Hilton used it to bash the Democratic supermajority control of Sacramento.

“The definition of insanity is believing that the people who put the red tape in place are somehow going to cut it,” he argued.

Hilton also pressed Becerra with specific questions about his record. When Becerra promised he would “cut red tape” to get more housing built, Hilton challenged him to name a time he had actually done so. The best he offered was his 2019 lawsuit against Huntington Beach for failing to meet state housing requirements, which is enforcing a mandate, not cutting regulations.

On affordability, the issue voters rank first, Hilton was crisp and consistent.

“The quickest way to get more money in people’s pockets is for the government to take less out,” he said.

On housing: “The quickest way to reduce the cost of housing is for the government to stop making it more expensive,” he added.

One can quarrel with the numbers, as Becerra did, arguing Hilton’s tax cuts would mostly help the wealthy and that Hilton’s “math doesn’t add up.” Hilton has said he’d pay for them by cutting high-speed rail, homelessness nonprofits, and 5% from all state departments’ budgets.

Hilton, whose lack of a necktie didn’t diminish his British accent, seems an unlikely populist. But he landed several punches while highlighting Becerra’s role as the Democratic establishment’s default choice.

“Xavier Becerra, you’re the candidate who is supported by the machine in Sacramento – the unions, big business, all these people that, for 16 years, have given us the highest cost of living in the country, made it impossible to build anything, given us the highest unemployment rate, the highest poverty rate.”

Becerra’s best moment

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra went after Hilton over federal enforcement raids, which are unpopular in California: “Steve thinks it’s perfect to let ICE mercenaries come on into California, and he welcomes it.”

Hilton responded by criticizing Becerra’s own record at HHS, where the department lost track of thousands of migrant children who had crossed the border alone.

“And you stand here lecturing people about immigration when you treated these most vulnerable children, unaccompanied children, in this way,” Hilton lectured.

He also reminded viewers that, as HHS secretary, Becerra kept a mask mandate in place for 2- and 3-year-olds in Head Start programs. Becerra’s half-hearted response was that he was following the medical experts’ advice at the time and that allowing “politicians” to dictate health policy is a fraught approach.

Becerra was at his most likable defending Hollywood. “We’ve got to keep Hollywood in Hollywood,” he said. “We don’t want it to be in Sydney, Australia. It shouldn’t be SydneyWood.”

Where Hilton came up short

As the underdog, Hilton had to make the most of a debate that will likely be the first and the last less than five weeks before Election Day. Yet, he was flatter than usual for stretches and neglected to highlight some of his interesting policy proposals and campaign promises, including lowering gas prices to $3 a gallon, eliminating taxes for people making less than $150,000, and cutting utility bills in half.

Hilton, who has spent the past year touring all 58 California counties, including Latino-majority cities most Republicans skip, also failed to press Becerra on the question that gave Kamala Harris the most trouble in her failed 2024 presidential campaign: What’s one thing you would do different than your predecessor?

Some of his swings landed hard. He read out former Obama and Biden adviser Susan Rice’s reported description of Becerra as an “idiot” and a “bitch-ass.” Becerra had no real response, simply waving it off: “Since when do I have to respond to politicians?”

That’s an incongruous line from a man who has been a career politician for 30 years, and it left Rice’s harsh verdict sitting there unanswered.

Yet, Hilton seemed surprised by some of the questions. He wandered into the weeds on vaccines, saying he supports vaccines but wants more parental discretion. That’s a defensible, nuanced position, but it’s not the type of punchy one-liner that rallies conservative base voters and wins over independents.

His housing pitch, built around counties bidding to host brand-new communities, is a bold idea that sounds great in a policy paper, but is difficult to convey in a 60-second answer.

Hilton is at his best when he keeps it simple: Costs are too high, Sacramento made them that way, and the people who did it are asking for four more years.

In the end, Hilton never fully shook the Trump label Becerra spent the night stitching onto him. He has said on the trail that “you can be anti-Trump and still vote for me.” He needed to explain why on Wednesday.

Where Becerra faltered

The low blow of the night was Becerra’s. Cornered on immigration, he turned personal and racial, telling Hilton, who emigrated from England: “You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you, but deport immigrants who look like me.” The suggestion that Hilton only wants white legal immigrants was a cheap shot, and Hilton chided his opponent for the racially divisive play.

“What a disgraceful remark that was,” he responded.

The AI exchange went little better. Hilton questioned whether Becerra could be trusted to regulate the industry, asking how much his campaign had taken in campaign contributions from OpenAI and Anthropic. Instead of answering, Becerra rattled off a list of other tech companies he had sued – Meta, Amazon, and Google – which was not the question.

Homelessness produced the night’s biggest surprise. Becerra promised to clear every homeless encampment in the state, a tougher line than any prominent California Democrat has taken. But he offered no specific plan for actually reducing homelessness. He promised to keep up “investments” in homeless services while focusing on addiction and mental illness, which is the same prescription Newsom has been writing for years.

Becerra never explained why that approach would work now. California has spent more than $24 billion on homelessness under Newsom, the problem has barely budged, and the spending has produced some egregious cases of fraud. Hilton cornered him on it, reminding viewers that during the spring primary debates Becerra gave Newsom an “A for effort” on homelessness. Few Californians who step over tents on their way to work would grade it that way.

Becerra never offered anything that sounded like a new idea or an original thought. His campaign refrain, that he is “not running on inflated promises,” is a nice line for a frontrunner, but hardly aspirational. Nearly every answer became another attack on Trump, which is not an answer to California’s problems.

There was some talk about housing, health insurance, and AI in state government. There was no big picture of what California looks like in 2030 under a Becerra administration, or why it would look different from the last 16 years.

One notable moment of agreement: both men oppose the billionaire wealth tax on the November ballot, even though most California Democrats support it.

Will it change anything?

Let’s be honest about the electoral math and the possible impact of one debate. Becerra led 60% to 38% in the latest mid-September Public Policy Institute of California poll, and 58% to 33% in the UC Berkeley IGS late August poll. Mail ballots start landing within days. Partly because Becerra has run a sleepy campaign, voters are mostly tuned out, and this debate did little to draw them in for the final weeks.

Still, despite Becerra’s lead, Hilton is asking the right questions, tapping into a high level of deep dissatisfaction Californians are feeling as costs continue to rise along with distrust in basic government competence. In the latest PPI survey a majority of likely California voters said the state is headed in the wrong direction.

Hilton’s best moments came when he asked the simple question: If you’re unhappy with how California is going, why keep voting for the people who got you here?

Becerra never answered it. Given the huge advantage Democrats enjoy in California, he was banking on the likelihood that doesn’t have to.
news.summary: In debate, Dem who wants to be governor complained about president 40 times

news.title: In Boston Freedom Rally speech, Greenfield resident urges voters not to repeal recreational cannabis law
news.text:
GREENFIELD — Ahead of the Nov. 3 election, when voters will consider repealing laws that legalized recreational cannabis, one Greenfield resident traveled nearly 100 miles to urge listeners at the Sept. 19 Boston Freedom Rally to vote against the proposed changes.

Voters will soon be asked to weigh in on repealing laws that allow for the sale, regulation and taxation of recreational cannabis. According to the Secretary of State’s Office, the proposed changes would allow people ages 21 and older to possess or give to someone else 1 ounce or less of marijuana that includes no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and impose a $100 civil penalty and forfeiture of the product for possession of marijuana weighing between 1 and 2 ounces.

As for the commercial impact, the proposed law, which would take effect Jan. 1, 2028, would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would also shift the authority of the state Cannabis Control Commission to only regulate the medical marijuana market.

“We are told the battle is won here in Massachusetts,” Greenfield resident Erika McGee told the crowd gathered at the Boston Common, “but we know the truth: true cognitive liberty is still on trial in this country. … No one handed a permission slip to the government giving them the right to police your consciousness. They took it!”

Wearing green lipstick, sunglasses with lenses in the shape of cannabis leaves, a green shirt with a cannabis leaf and a necklace of cannabis leaf garlands, she listed politicians who have mentioned memories of using cannabis, including former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg, former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris and former U.S. President Barack Obama.

“While they get to joke about it on the campaign trail, countless everyday people lost their families, their livelihoods and their loved ones to the violent enforcement of the war on drugs,” McGee said. “It isn’t just political hypocrisy — it is a human tragedy, and we are tired of the double standard!”

McGee started using cannabis in her 30s as a way to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). She remembers sitting at home smoking marijuana, when a question hit her.

“Wait, who gave people permission to tell me that I can’t change my consciousness?” she recalled thinking. Speaking of the federal government, she said, “They’ve made nature a criminal, and a crime for us to interact with it. … That’s something I could not comprehend.”

In 2016, her first year living in Greenfield, she started volunteering with the Massachusetts Cannabis Reform Coalition, the group behind the Boston Freedom Rally.

The rally started in 1989 in North Adams, nearly 30 years before Massachusetts voters approved decriminalizing recreational cannabis use. According to the Massachusetts Cannabis Reform Coalition’s website, the rally “brings together advocates, activists and the public to raise awareness, support reform and celebrate cannabis culture while fostering a deeper understanding of its potential benefits.”

“It was such an incredible experience,” McGee wrote in an email after the rally. “I did what I was invited to do, and I am ecstatic to represent western Mass.”

Iowa Republican gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn said Saturday that mobilizing Republican voters and pressing Democrat opponent Rob Sand on his policy positions would guide his campaign’s final month, while crediting Republican leadership with helping attract an announced $15 billion steel plant investment to the state.

Speaking in an exclusive interview on Breitbart News Saturday, Lahn told host Matthew Boyle that the election carries stakes beyond individual policies or economic proposals. “This is a fight for the culture of our state and our country,” he said.

Boyle opened the interview by asking about President Donald Trump’s announcement of a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, describing it as a “huge, huge, huge development” and asking how Lahn would help get the project operating if elected governor.

“This is a huge announcement,” Lahn said. “$15 billion into an economically depressed area of the state, southeast Iowa, is going to bring manufacturing jobs, highest quality steel in America, right to Iowa.”

Lahn said Iowa secured the investment over neighboring states because of its approach to governance and business. “Illinois didn’t get it. Iowa got it because we have good, stable governance. We are very business friendly,” he said, crediting the legislature and governor with promoting that environment.

“As governor, I’m going to continue to promote business” and bring companies into Iowa, Lahn said, adding that he would place an even greater emphasis on investing in “Iowa’s homegrown businesses.”

Lahn said the plant will create “2,000 new jobs” and could affect southeastern Iowa for decades. “This is a 40-, 50-, 60-year plant that we’re looking at that’s going to change a region of the state, and I think Iowa is very, very happy to get it,” he said.

Boyle asked Lahn how important his election would be for voters who want to see the steel plant “up, operational quickly, and the jobs coming in in a big way.”

Lahn responded by criticizing Sand’s tax positions and political alliances. “My opponent is beholden to very radical people on the left,” he said. “There has not been any tax cut that Iowa has done in modern history that he’s supported. He’s criticized all of them.”

Lahn emphasized that cooperation with Trump was also necessary for the steel project, saying it “required being able to work with the president of the United States on this plan and this project.” He accused Democrats nationally of being unwilling to work with Trump “even if it would benefit their constituents.”

In Lahn’s assessment, resistance to Trump could have cost Iowa the investment. “It would have picked a state that was more friendly to the project,” he said, crediting “the past 10 years of Republican leadership” with helping bring the state to the point of securing a $15 billion investment.

Boyle asked Lahn what voters should expect at his debate against Sand on Tuesday, also mentioning a photograph Lahn had posted showing his Democrat opponent wearing a Biden-Harris face mask. “That’s not AI, by the way,” Lahn said.

Lahn replied that he intended to press Sand on positions he said the Democrat no longer addresses publicly. “The voters of Iowa deserve to understand where my opponent stands on the issues that he will not talk about anymore,” he said, citing benefits for illegal immigrants, support for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s Green New Deal, gun control, and partial-birth abortion.

Lahn characterized Sand as “a radically liberal Democrat that is running as a moderate,” saying the debate would give voters an opportunity to examine those radical positions. “I think we’re going to have a good and lively debate,” he said. “I think it’ll be very productive.”

Boyle also asked about support from Trump and Vice President JD Vance, along with polling in the governor’s race, referencing Ann Selzer’s preelection Iowa poll in 2024. Lahn said Selzer “was off by 16 points, I believe, nearly 17 points.”

Lahn attributed current polling problems to difficulty getting Republicans to participate. “You cannot get Republicans to take the polls,” he said, contending that polls were interviewing more Kamala Harris voters than Trump voters “in a state that Donald Trump won by 13 points.”

“Just that fact alone means that you can’t trust the numbers that are coming out,” Lahn said. He also asserted that polls can be used to encourage Democrats and discourage Republicans, saying, “They want to give more hope, and they want to depress Republicans,” and comparing that effect to political betting markets.

Lahn contrasted those polling concerns with attendance at campaign events. “We’re having hundreds of people show up to town halls and rallies that we’re doing across the state,” he said.

Discussing Vance’s recent appearance in Council Bluffs, Lahn described the vice president’s speech as “very rousing” and “energetic,” saying, “The majority of it was about my race because they understand what’s at stake here.”

Lahn said he hoped Trump would also visit Iowa and help mobilize supporters. “It really is a turnout battle for Iowa,” he said, arguing that Republicans could win by achieving participation levels that are “normal for a cycle like this.”

As Boyle emphasized Republican voter registration strength, Lahn said Iowa has “over 180,000” more registered Republicans than Democrats, adding, “These are real numbers.”

Asked about his plan for the campaign’s final four weeks, Lahn pointed to direct engagement with voters. “Iowa is a retail politics state. It’s how we won the primary,” he said, describing his primary victory as “the biggest upset in the country” and predicting his general election race would be among the larger upsets.

Lahn said his primary campaign held “50, 60 town halls,” with attendance growing from eight people at the first event to between 200 and 300 at later gatherings. “You have to get in front of the people,” he said.

Although fundraising and advertising remain necessary, Lahn argued that television, radio, and mail have “a diminishing return as you get closer to the election,” particularly amid spending on Iowa’s Senate race, governor’s race, and three contested House races.

“That’s what we’re going to be doing for the last 30 days of this campaign — is getting directly in front of the people” and delivering the campaign’s message, Lahn said. He added that the state party and outside groups were “all focused on getting the vote out.”

Lahn said those organizations were committing more money and resources than ever to turnout efforts “because we just have to get Republicans to show up.”

While defending Republican leadership, Lahn also acknowledged areas in which he believes the state needs to improve. “We’ve had a Republican governor and legislature for 10 years, and I’m running on things we need to improve because there are things we need to improve,” he said.

Lahn framed the election as a question of the state’s future and quality of life. “We are fighting to preserve and protect the culture because this is not all just an economic discussion,” he said. “There’s also the quality of life. What do you want your state to look like?”

Asked whether Iowans were offended by national Democrats moving South Carolina ahead of Iowa in their presidential nominating process, Lahn responded, “Well, yes,” saying the party had become “hardly recognizable” and was run by “rich coastal elites” who “view Iowa in the Midwest with disdain.”

Lahn said Republicans had maintained Iowa’s early role because they recognize “the common sense values, the Heartland values that come from the state of Iowa, and they want to maintain that.”

When Boyle asked how listeners could help during the final weeks, Lahn recounted a personal connection to Breitbart. “When I was in college, I actually wrote for Breitbart a long time ago,” he said, adding that he knew Andrew Breitbart “fairly well.”

In reply to Boyle’s question, Lahn urged listeners with connections to Iowa to explain the election’s stakes to Iowans. “Right now, I have an opponent that’s running as a moderate, but has radically liberal views, and he’s not being honest about who he is,” he said.

“If you’re in Iowa, make sure you’re getting in touch with your friends and neighbors and getting them to vote,” Lahn said. For listeners elsewhere who have friends in the state, he added, “Let them know what’s going on.”

Lahn also pointed to the Senate contest between Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, recalling a mailer he said he received as a registered Republican. The mailer, he said, described how Turek was “going to work with Donald Trump to seal the border.”

Lahn accused Democrats of trying to persuade Republican voters that they shared their positions. “This is the type of lies that are being put out to try to fool Republicans into thinking that they’re one of them, and it’s happening all across the country,” he said.

He closed by urging listeners to vote and communicate with others about the race. “We have to make sure that we are fighting to protect the culture of our state and our country,” Lahn said.

news.title: Races For Senate And House In Five Traditional Republican States Will Be Close: Poll
news.text: Races for the Senate and House in five key traditionally Republican-leaning states will be close as Donald Trump's approval ratings continue to sink, a new poll has shown.In the Senate races, the Democrat candidate edges out the Republican by a margin of 50 percent to 43 percent in Alaska, 49 percent to 46 percent in Ohio, 51 percent to 45 percent in Texas, a New York Times/Siena survey conducted between September 21st and October 1st showed.The Texas race is a particularly high-profile one, as a victory for Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton would mark the first time a Texas Democrat has won election to the U.S. Senate since Lloyd Bentsen's victory in 1988.In Kansas, the Republican and Democrat candidates are tied on 45 percent, whereas in Iowa the Republican candidate maintains a narrow lead of 48 percent compared to the Democrat's 47.The congressional polls showed a more complicated picture, with Republican candidates ahead by three points in Iowa and 5 points in Kansas respectively. In both Texas and Ohio, the Democrat candidates lead the Republicans by 48 percent to 47 percent.All five states surveyed voted for Republican President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, which the poll reflects.The proportion of respondents who voted for Trump in 2024, which ranges from 45 percent in Alaska to 49 percent in Iowa and Kansas, is much higher than the proportion who voted for 2024 Democrat presidential candidate Kamala Harris, which ranges from 36 percent in Alaska to 41 percent in Ohio.However, the president's approval ratings have been sinking, even in more Republican-leaning areas.According to the poll, between 48 percent and 51 percent of voters in all five states strongly disapprove of the way that Trump is handling the job of president. In contrast, Trump's highest "strong approval" score in the five states was recorded in Alaska (29 percent) and his lowest came in Ohio (21 percent).This disapproval appears to extend to traditional Republican voters, as more voters identified themselves as Republicans than Democrats in all five states, reflecting the states' historically conservative ideological lean.The economy featured highest on voters' priorities, with 21 percent of respondents citing it as the issue most important in deciding which candidates to back. It is perhaps unsurprising that this prioritization of economic issues is coinciding with a fall in support for Trump, as recent polls have also shown that Trump's approval ratings on the economy are lower than his predecessor President Joe Biden's were.
news.summary: A poll of nearly 3000 voters in Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Kansas and Iowa showed that, overall, Democrat candidates are gaining ground ahead of November's midterm elections.

news.title: From Democratic insider to party exile: Lindy Li isn’t ruling out another run for Congress
news.text: Before raising millions of campaign dollars for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris or breaking ranks with the Democratic Party to publish a tell-all political memoir, Lindy Li was trying to build a political career from the candidate’s podium. "I just knew," Li said. "I knew that I was supposed to run for Congress. But I didn’t know I was supposed to do it at twenty-four years old." In the lead-up to the 2024 election, that ambition crashed headlong into lifelong convictions about loyalty and stretched them to a breaking point. Li’s status as a top Democratic fundraiser would soon crumble as she switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election. That break has left her uncertain about her future, but hasn’t stopped her from thinking about what could come next. EX-DEM INSIDER REVEALS SHE WILL EXPOSE DEMOCRATS WHO COVERED UP BIDEN'S COGNITIVE DECLINE IN NEW BOOK. "President Rubio calls me in two years, four years, then there's an open seat in Pennsylvania for whatever reason," Li said, ruminating about her future. "You know, I could solidify my hand on a hundred million dollars. I think few people could do a better job, and I'm sorry if that sounds conceited. And I'm not saying I want it; I'm just saying if it falls into my lap, then sure, but who knows?" Li’s family initially came to the United States from China, fleeing persecution from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which Li said had killed her great-grandfather. After growing up briefly in Sheffield, England, Li joined her parents in New England at the age of five. She recounted how her family moved from Boston to New Haven to Pennsylvania as her father worked as a doctor. From her parents, Li said she inherited a sense of work ethic that enabled her to fuel her sense of political destiny. At Princeton, Li used that work ethic to become the only woman class president to hold the office for four consecutive years. "I used to go around with candy and just be like, ‘Can you please vote for me? This is what I intend to do. I want to expand late meals and offer sushi,’ whatever the platform was. I was tenacious; nobody could outwork me," Li said. EX-DEM INSIDER BLOWS LID OFF FUNDRAISING 'GIMMICKS' DURING 2024 ELECTION: 'PYRAMID SCHEME' The "plan," Li said, was to become a senator. But that wasn’t supposed to happen for another ten years when, in 2012, a school shooter attacked Sandy Hook Elementary School, killing 20 children. Li recalled how the attack accelerated her convictions to enter public life and prompted her to leave a budding career in finance. "I just felt it in my heart that I was supposed to help do whatever I could to save those kids," Li said. Despite conservative leanings, Li ran twice as a Democrat, never advancing past the primary stage. But her fundraising caught the attention of Democratic strategists. In 2016, she raised nearly $515,000 and in 2018 another $168,000. "I didn't intend to become a fundraiser," Li recalled. "It's a lot of salesmanship, and I hated it. I hate it. And I also know I'm very good at it. This is not me bragging; I just know." "They came to my home. I remember. The executive director showed up to my home to recruit me for this. It was like Scientology. He noticed— I mean, everybody noticed that as a kid I basically raised $700,000. I just caught the eye of party leadership." Alongside her aspirations, Li said she also cultivated a sense of loyalty, a quality she said has been a key part of her character since she can remember. "Like if somebody's kind to me, I will go to the ends of the earth for them. And it always surprises me and I shouldn't be surprised when someone doesn't reciprocate because that's just how I operate. You have to give me a reason to walk away from you. If you have my loyalty, there's very little I wouldn't do for you," Li said. That loyalty, combined with her fundraising prowess, led Li to climb swiftly, rubbing shoulders with some of the party’s top operatives. During the Biden and Harris campaigns, Li communicated with figures like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., — many of whom she built personal relationships with. But that loyalty reached a tipping point in 2024 when, as a fundraiser, Li saw the party selling donors and voters on the idea that President Joe Biden could serve effectively as president for another four years despite mounting concerns about his cognitive abilities. In recent months, Li has published a book, Unbroken, documenting the party’s internal deliberations around Biden’s age and how, according to her, many of them knowingly understood the political liabilities that came with his age. EX-DEM INSIDER REVEALS WHY BIDEN'S DAUGHTER THREATENED TO SUE HER: 'BORDERED ON PARODY' That book and the warpath to writing it have severed virtually all of her relationships from when she was a Democrat. As she documented in her book, it even cost her a personal romantic relationship of eight years. To an extent, Li understood the price tag that came with her decision to go public with her insider knowledge. She suspects some of the people she left behind understand that price, too. "If Josh Shapiro ever walks into the room, I know we're gonna understand each other, I know. Like despite everything that's happened. I think he's going to understand. I understand why he needed to throw me, you know, to the wolves." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I never would have done that to him, though," she added. Li still holds fast to the idea of loyalty as a matter of personal conviction. But regardless of where her ambitions take her next, she believes she will have to temper them with honesty that makes few allowances for party narratives. news.title: Ex-Kamala Harris aide: Cornell wanted my voice. I gave it to Jane Doe
news.text:
I was scheduled to speak at Cornell University this fall. Students there had planned a thoughtful visit, and I was genuinely excited that an Ivy League school wanted to hear from me. I withdrew because, in good conscience, I couldn't show up on a campus facing serious questions about failing to protect its young women.A young woman, identified in court filings as Jane Doe, has alleged that seven fraternity members gang raped her. According to her lawsuit, some of the men made crude jokes about her in a Snapchat group, and not one of them did anything to help her. 

The allegations are horrifying. But what made my decision was what came after. Where are the institutions that are supposed to protect us? What I and many students see is them protecting themselves, their reputations, their donors and their power. 

My decision had nothing to do with the students who invited me. It was about a crucial promise the university appears to have failed to keep. When I was a resident adviser in college, I was the person whose door students were supposed to be able to knock on at 2 a.m. I remember meeting parents on move-in day who dropped off their daughters believing the school would keep them safe. Jane Doe says Cornell didn't keep that promise.

Cornell wouldn't be the first university to fail a survivor

I've seen how rarely consequences come on their own. In 2016, I was on the advance team for Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign when a 2005 recording surfaced of Donald Trump bragging about touching women, in a way most of us took as sexual assault. 

I remember waiting for the consequences. They never came. In 2023, a federal jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing E. Jean Carroll. The next year, he was elected president again.

So what's the lesson for young people watching? You can hurt women and still rise to the top. And if you're one of the men standing by, you can stay quiet, and nothing will ever be asked of you.

If Jane Doe's allegations prove true, Cornell won't be the first university to fail a survivor. I think about Chanel Miller at Stanford University, and about all the women who told the truth only to watch people decide it was easier not to hear it.

Cornell's owes Jane Doe a complete investigation 

Universities work hard to win over the people around them. They want speakers who bring credibility, alumni who give and families who trust them with their children and their tuition. That gives all of us leverage, and we rarely use it. Speakers can weigh their invitations. Alumni can ask what their university is doing for survivors before writing the next check. Parents can ask on the campus tour what happens when a student reports an assault. We get to decide which rooms we lend our names to, and we should expect more of the institutions that want them.

Pressure works. This past week, Jane Doe's criminal case has been reopened, and New York Attorney General Letitia James has taken over as special prosecutor. I believe that happened because people refused to look away, like the brave student journalists at The Cornell Daily Sun who had the courage to pursue this story.Cornell owes Jane Doe more than silence. The university owes the former student an independent investigation, something which it has agreed to. That investigation should include how Cornell handled her report, public findings and a clear plan so that the next student who comes forward is protected, not managed.

This isn't only an American problem. In India, where my family is from, a string of recently reported sexual assaults in and around Delhi has been met with calls for more women-only train cars and buses. 

Here in America, we tell women not to wear short skirts, to carry pepper spray, to share their live location. Everywhere, the answer is for women to shrink. When are we going to ask men to be better, and ask the same of the institutions entrusted with our daughters?

I believe Jane Doe. The rest of us get to decide whether we'll hold Cornell, and every institution like it, to the promise it made.Opal Vadhan is the founder of Opal Office, a strategic advisory firm. She was a senior adviser to Vice President Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton's trip director.

news.title: Republicans Face Midterms Disaster—What Polling Reveals
news.text: With exactly one month until Election Day, Republicans are confronting what appears to be an increasingly precarious political map, as polling and election forecasters show Democratic candidates competitive or ahead in several races that could determine control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats are hoping polling surges and low approval ratings for President Donald Trump help them ride a massive blue wave into the majority in both the House and the Senate. Republicans hope the president hitting the campaign trail can boost turnout among their base and stave off Democratic gains. Voters head to the polls on November 3, with every House seat and 35 Senate contests on the ballot. Democrats need to pick up four seats each in both the House and the Senate to gain control of the chambers. Political forecasters like Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball have shifted numerous races toward Democrats, and though many contests remain within tight and within polling margins of error, the emerging picture raises the prospect of substantial Republican losses. The generic ballot—which assesses how a typical politician would fare in a race based just on party—puts Democrats ahead by over eight points, according to RealClearPolitics' polling average. In the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term in office, Democrats rode a blue wave to a net gain of 41 seats in the House, but they were not able to sustain that momentum against a difficult Senate map, ultimately seeing the GOP expand its majority from 51 seats to 53. The map appeared similar in 2026, with only two Republican seats being defended in states that Democratic nominee Kamala Harris won in 2024, but the battleground has expanded to longtime GOP strongholds amid voters' dissatisfaction with the economy, inflation and the Iran war. Senate Polls Show Republican Seats at Risk A polling snapshot from Election Central, updated September 28, showed Democrats leading in six Republican-held Senate contests—Alaska, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. And four major election forecasters—FiftyPlusOne, Silver Bulletin, Split Ticket, and VoteHub—predict that all five of those races (taking out Iowa) favor Democrats. Despite the GOP currently holding North Carolina, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper has taken such a commanding lead over his opponent, former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley, that NBC reports that the GOP's top Senate super PAC has paused spending in the race. If each party won every other seat they are expected to hold, victories in those six races would put Democrats above the four-seat gain needed for Senate control. These figures are a snapshot, however, and not a forecast. Several of the margins were narrow. Newsweek contacted the National Republican Senatorial Committee for comment on the midterms and was directed to reporting by CNN noting that polling of MAGA Republicans indicates high enthusiasm for the election. Additionally, the NRSC pointed to analysis by conservative pollster Patrick Ruffini showing that Senate polling from 2018–2024 overstated Democratic turnout in Iowa, Ohio, and Michigan “Democrats should think twice before relying too heavily on the same rosy polling that has historically written Republicans off cycle after cycle," NRSC National press secretary Bernadette Breslin said in prior statements. “To the doomsdayers and prognosticators out there, the GOP base is poised to show up at the polls in full force this November." Polling has shown Democrats with momentum and it has driven donor dollars. In Alaska, former Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola has raised over $18.5 million in her challenge against incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan. Currently, the RealClearPolitics' polling average gives her a one-and-a-half-point lead over Sullivan. Similarly, in Iowa—a state that has not voted Democratic at the presidential level since 2012 and has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008—Democratic State Representative Josh Turek holds a half-point lead over Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson despite her lead in fundraising, $10.2 million to $6.3 million The Senate race in Texas has become especially problematic for the GOP. Marist put Democratic state Representative James Talarico six points ahead of the state’s Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton on September 23, although a Republican-aligned Pulse Decision Science poll later showed Paxton leading by three. Democrats were last competitive in Texas back in 2018 amidst the candidacy of former Congressman Beto O'Rourke. However, O'Rourke led in a few polls during that time, while Talarico leads in most. The turnaround of Texas has long been talked about by Democrats and they say they have created a statewide campaign infrastructure that was not there before. "The [party] resources were almost nothing,” O’Rourke told Newsweek. “We just had to do that all from scratch.” In Ohio, Marist found Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown leading incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted 51 percent to 43 percent. Elected to the Senate in 2007, Brown served the state for 18 years until he lost to Republican challenger Bernie Moreno in 2024. The seat he's running for this cycle was the one Husted was appointed to fill for Vice President JD Vance. Brown still holds superior name recognition, and The New York Times reported that some voters believe he is still the incumbent. Husted also must contend with the voters' turn on data centers, something he once celebrated as bringing jobs to Ohio. The Maine Senate race remains very close. Late-September polling ranged from GOP Senator Susan Collins leading former Democratic State Senator Troy Jackson by three points to Jackson leading by four or five. Jackson became the nominee after controversial candidate Graham Platner dropped out amid sexual assault allegations. Collins has served the state since 1997 and has continually fended off strong challenges, but Jackson hopes his working-class bona fides will align with Maine's shifting politics. “Democrats are fighting for the [working class],” Jackson told Newsweek in an interview. “They’re fighting for them every day, but you don’t hear them talking about it because we don’t talk about our priorities to the extent that we need to. We just need to get back to economics.” Harris took Maine in 2024, and it is the only seat available for Democrats to flip in a state where they topped Trump. Democrats must also defend several of their own seats The two states they most need to protect are Michigan and New Hampshire. A Trafalgar survey showed Democratic Representative Chris Pappas six points ahead of former Republican Senator John Sununu in New Hampshire. In Michigan, Marist placed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed seven points ahead of former GOP Representative Mike Rogers in Michigan. “This race is top versus down, and [Rogers] has been on top for far too long, trading on his relationships to people in power to make money to go golfing with his buddies," El-Sayed told Newsweek in an interview. "The way that I explain Donald Trump is that people were so sick and tired of the establishment on either side of the parties." Election Forecasters Shift Toward Democrats The shifts extend beyond the Senate. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted 11 House races toward Democrats on September 29, following eight Democratic shifts two weeks earlier. Its September 22 update also moved Michigan’s Senate race to “Leans Democratic” while identifying Democratic movement in Iowa and even Kansas. Those changes suggest the Republican problem is no longer confined to a handful of races. The National Republican Congressional Committee did not return Newsweek's request for comment, but in an October 2 appearance on Fox, NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson said, "We have a battlefield, a map that favors Republicans. We’ve got better candidates. We’ve gone out and recruited some of the best candidates we’ve ever had." Which Republican House Seats Are Most at Risk? The Republican-held House seats facing the greatest danger include seats in Arizona, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia, where election forecasters have recently shifted races toward Democrats. A larger second tier of toss-ups stretches through California, Colorado, Iowa, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Texas and Wisconsin. The most vulnerable seats are Arizona’s 1st Congressional District and New Jersey’s 7th District. On September 25, the Cook Political Report moved both from “Toss Up” to “Lean Democratic,” signaling that Democrats had gained a discernible, although not decisive, advantage. Arizona’s seat is open following Representative David Schweikert’s retirement, while Republican Representative Thomas Kean Jr., who was absent from Congress for several months earlier this year, is seeking reelection in New Jersey. Beyond those Democratic-leaning contests, Cook Political Report classifies 16 Republican-held seats as toss-ups: That imbalance is central to the fight for control of the lower chamber. Sixteen of Cook Political Report’s 22 toss-ups are Republican-held, compared with six Democratic-held seats, and many of these seats are favored by some forecasters to flip Democrat. According to VoteHub, all those seats lean toward Democrats. However, the two Michigan seats have just a slight tilt. Why Congressioanl Control Matters A shift in the House majority would have consequences beyond the number of Republican seats lost. The majority party elects the Speaker, controls committee leadership and determines which legislation reaches the floor. A Democratic House could constrain the Republican administration during its final two years, increase congressional investigations and block parts of the president’s legislative agenda. Many House Democrats have indicated a desire to impeach Trump. If the left takes the majority, impeachment could become possible. If Democrats take the Senate, the president could face a very politically painful impeachment trial, even if they don't have the 60 votes required to remove him from office. Many of Trump's hopes for the second term could hinge on these election results. For more analysis from us on the numbers shaping U.S. politics and the 2026 midterms, sign up for Newsweek's Midterms Monitor newsletter. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to help produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: In one month, Americans will decide control of Congress. If current polling proves correct, Republicans will face a brutal night.

news.title: With 'SubwayTakes' in Toronto, viral interviews rewrite rules of celeb promotion
news.text:
In October, the viral digital interview series “SubwayTakes” will debut a series of Toronto episodes filmed on the TTC. The jokes about host Kareem Rahma and the folks on the other end of his Presto-card-mounted microphone getting stuck between stations — especially during rush hour — write themselves. (“He needs to do it on Line 2 for the real good s—t,” read one popular post on X.)

The premise of “SubwayTakes” riffs on a long tradition of person-on-the-street interviews. Clad in an oversized suit and sunglasses that comprise a kind of hipster-verité ensemble, Rahma tosses out possible talking points — the more trivial the better — to strangers and celebrities and positions himself as a devil’s advocate. A few classic examples: “The government should pay for people’s parents to go to therapy”; “Nobody should be allowed to wear shorts”; “Naps are disgusting.” The goal is for each participant to convince the other, and no less than fully: the minimum threshold for agreement is 100 per cent.

The tension between the potential elasticity of the subject matter and the adversarial nature of the setup explains the show’s popularity, and at its best, “SubwayTakes” channels the tetchy exhilaration of picking a hill and dying on it. “The show came out of my love of debate and discussion,” Rahma, a Cairo-born comedian and former New York Times editor, who’s honed his conversational skills into a minor media empire, has said.

For the first year of its existence, “SubwayTakes” thrived on underdog appeal; the comedians, musicians and online personalities in the mix were niche figures. The first time Zohran Mamdani chopped it up with Rahma on the G train, he was barely a blip on the national political radar.

By 2024, though, “Subway Takes” was popular enough to attract Kamala Harris, whose appearance was (in)famously shelved after the Democratic presidential candidate went off script. In a set of interviews after the fact, Rahma explained that Harris’ “take” — that “bacon is a spice” — was “confusing and weird” even by the series’ proudly esoteric standards; her campaign was apparently happy to have the footage scuttled as well.

The widening ratio of well-known guests to civilians on “SubwayTakes” is part of a larger shift in the celeb-promotion ecosystem — a recently minted cycle of goofy intimacy and self-deprecating humiliation rituals that have supplanted magazine cover stories and broadcast TV segments.

Rahma’s satisfaction in enlisting A-listers like Charli xcx and Jennifer Lopez to wax philosophical about nothing in particular is palpable. It means his subterranean show is upwardly mobile.

Cate Blanchett as the format’s MVP

The two-way exchange on “SubwayTakes” is fascinating. On the one hand, famous people validate — and elevate — Rahma’s setup; on the other, the cramped visuals and digressive interview confer a sense of accessibility. It’s always beguiling to see an icon humanized. Case in point: Cate Blanchett, during her 2025 appearance, inveighed with perfect, Oscar-worthy diction against the scourge of leaf blowers; squint, and she could have been just another crank in the middle of a commute. “The rise of cardiac problems has gone through the roof because people are not doing the physical exercise (of raking),” she insisted. Fair enough.

A case can be made for Blanchett as the MVP of the 21st-century pop-up promotional circuit. In addition to her star turn on “SubwayTakes,” she’s held court in the Criterion Closet — perhaps the purest example of high-end clout chasing, with entrants transformed instantly into cinephiles by snatching up free Blu-rays — and scorched her palate opposite Sean Evans on “Hot Ones.”

All that’s missing for Blanchett to add the viral-talk-show equivalent of an EGOT to her resumé is a stint on “Chicken Shop Date” opposite cringe-interviewer extraordinaire Amelia Dimoldenberg, like Rahma a breakout star of the content-creator era. Sadly, that show will be wrapping its run before she gets the chance. (The real dream would have been for Blanchett to go on in character as Lydia Tár).

By now, it’s an accepted piece of industry wisdom that the overall paradigm has shifted away from staid studio shooting and in the direction of relaxed, algorithmic absurdism — possibly permanently. Call it the rise of the small-talk show. The New Yorker dubbed “Subway Takes” the “TikTok version of the ‘Tonight Show,’” a nifty distillation of its appeal.

The premise of “Hot Ones” — a star obligingly chokes down a sampler platter of thermonuclear-seasoned chicken wings while trying to stay poised and on topic — is worth deconstructing in this context: it literalizes the idea of bite-sized entertainment. When chef Gordon Ramsay showed up on “Hot Ones” to stare down host Evans in 2019, it felt like a passing of the foodie-influencer torch (or drumette). “I don’t know whether to sneeze, fart or piss myself,” moaned the “Hell’s Kitchen” star, dropping his guard in front of 137 million YouTube viewers.

A sense of intimacy and spontaneity

It’s probably ahistorical to suggest that shows like “Subway Takes” and “Hot Ones” are truly inventing anything: Johnny Carson knew how to disarm his guests, and David Letterman was a master of stupid human tricks as well as pet ones.

Still, the sense of intimacy and spontaneity on offer in these content-creator-driven showcases is undeniable. They provide a spicy — or, in the case of Amy Poehler’s new podcast, “Good Hang,” a sticky-sweet — antidote to the blandishments of the old-school promotional circuit. Compare, for instance, Robert De Niro’s notoriously tight-lipped demeanour during print interviews — exemplified by a 2006 GQ piece in which the writer was forced to count the words uttered by his subject (972) — with his open-hearted appearance opposite Poehler, who unexpectedly reduced her guest to tears while praising his public advocacy. (“This is going to be a real switcheroo,” Poehler said, “because I can’t believe I just made you cry.”) Or Tom Cruise’s glee at getting to resurrect his “Risky Business” shtick on Jennifer Hudson’s “Spirit Tunnel” versus his own recent blood-from-a-stone GQ feature.

So far, the guest slate for the Toronto “SubwayTakes” is a mystery, save for Mike Myers, who was spotted pirouetting through the Bloor-Yonge station in August (surely with his elbows up). Whether one feels good about the possibility that Rahma’s enterprise represents the future of talk shows — or anxious that it’s just so much short-attention-span theatre — it’s worth debating, 100 per cent.

news.title: Young voters swung to Trump in 2024. Now they are leaning Democratic
news.text:
A key group of voters who swung towards President Donald Trump in 2024 are now swinging just as sharply away from him ahead of the 2026 midterm elections: young people.

Nationwide polls of likely and registered voters from Economist/YouGov, Marquette Law School, Reuters/Ipsos, Emerson College and Echelon Insights showed that young voters have moved away from Trump more than other age groups have. The September polling showed Trump's approval among young voters ranged from 19.5% in Emerson's poll to 31% in Echelon Insight's poll, while his approval from the whole population ranged from 32% in the Reuters/Ipsos poll to 39% in Emerson's poll.

More: New poll shows more bad news for Trump's approval rating, good news for Dems

That comes only two years after Trump made gains among young voters, who are usually defined by pollsters as those under 30. Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the group 54% to 43%, according to exit polls, but Trump improved his youth vote performance compared to previous elections, especially among young men. In 2020, he only won 36% of the youth vote, so 2024 represented a 7 percentage-point improvement.

"There's sort of this reputation about Gen Z that they might not be engaged or care, and we've learned through listening they are a little bit jaded around our political process," said Kalisha Dessources, of the nonpartisan voter turnout organization When We All Vote.

When asked by pollsters whether they approve of Trump's performance and which party they would prefer in a congressional race, young people are more likely than voters 30 years old and up to say that they disapprove of the president and will vote a Democrat to Congress in the midterms.

Young voters more likely to be independent, struggling with cost of living

Young voters are less likely to affiliate themselves with a political party, according to experts, and they are expressing financial frustration at an even higher rate than the electorate as a whole.

"We're in this, like, new political era where younger people are judging their politicians and their politics and kind of how they think, voting through a different lens than previous cohorts," John Della Volpe, who leads a youth voter polling initiative at Harvard University, said.

Dissatisfaction with high inflation during the Biden era contributed to Trump's 2024 success, particularly among young voters, who earn less and have less savings than older Americans. According to the Bureau of Labor statistics, inflation sat at 2.7% in November 2024. As of August 2026, inflation has risen to 3.4%.

More: A 'blue wave' coming? What trends a new Marquette poll finds | Gilbert

Della Volpe has studied young voters since 2000 and called it a "stability and experience era" in which young voters are looking to politicians to help them lead a more stable day-to-day life, often in terms of financial security.

He runs focus groups around the country with young voters and shared the story of one young woman in Michigan telling him in the spring of 2024 that the election was going to be about the economy. She said she was leaning towards Trump because she could "worry about abortion and guns and other important issues" after her own economic situation was settled. 

A spokesperson for The Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University, which tracks engagement and voter trends among young people, told USA TODAY that the current young voter population is composed of "issues-based voters." That group of voters is more independent and are not judging every candidate in the Republican Party by their assessment of the Trump administration.

"The fact that they may be frustrated or disillusioned with the current administration doesn't necessarily mean that they're going to go ahead and vote in the other direction,"said CIRCLE's Alberto Medina. 

CIRCLE's tracking of young voters revealed that two-thirds said their political opinions have changed in recent years. Medina said that isn't surprising, given "young people are still kind of figuring things out and looking at their options and making choices based on the issues and what's happening around them." 

Dessources said that in When We All Vote's interactions with voters at summer events such as Lollapalooza and the World Cup, the organization also found the group to be more issues-based than partisan. Forty-three percent of Gen Z Americans surveyed at these events said that they identify as independents, and many expressed frustration with the cost of living. 

In Echelon Insights' polling, the cost of living was the top concern for all voters but "young voters are more likely to list that as their top issue," according to Avery James, the communications director for the polling organization. James noted, though, that during the 2022 midterms, then-President Joe Biden also had "a significant gap with younger and older voters as he was looking at the handling of the economy." 

In the Economist/YouGov September poll, 29% of Americans rated inflation as the most important problem. Among voters aged 18-29, 38% ranked inflation as the most important issue. In contrast, voters 65 and older were more likely to rank presidential leadership (17%) as their top issue, with only 6% of young voters who identified it as their top issue in the Economist/YouGov poll.

Just as young voters were more likely to disapprove of Trump, they're more likely to disapprove of his war in Iran. In the same poll, 63% of the electorate overall disapproved of the war and 31% approved. When it came to young voters, 69% disapproved and only 25% approved.

Young men told Della Volpe in his focus groups that "they were promised by Donald Trump... a lower cost of living and fewer wars."

Young men backed Trump rather than GOP

Exit polls from a consortium of news organizations in 2024 showed 49% of the young men voted for Trump, compared with 48% voting for Harris. CIRCLE at Tufts reports a much larger split, saying in their exit polling that 56% of young men voted for Trump and 42% voted for Harris.

The online "bro" podcast culture with MAGA media personalities like Joe Rogan and the Nelk Boys helped boost Trump with that demographic.

But a "bro vote" for Trump in 2024 didn't necessarily mean that young men were signing up to stick with the Republicans. A Sept. 15-18 poll by Cygnal of registered young male voters showed the Democratic congressional candidates in the midterms lead Republicans by almost 10 points. 

"Young men, in particular, played a key role in returning Donald Trump to the White House," said Della Volpe, of Harvard. "Almost two years later, the lesson from that experience in that election was that a vote for Donald Trump did not mean that younger people or younger men were signing up to be Republicans for life." 

Young voters are less likely to vote

One caveat that may soften the blow for Republicans: Young people are relatively unlikely to vote.

The data review by USA TODAY revealed that more than half of young voters reported being likely or enthusiastic to vote, but their response on those questions fell from 5 to 17 points below the polls' total percentage. 

According to Marquette Law School in September, only 56% of young voters were "absolutely certain” or "very likely" to vote, compared with 73% of the whole electorate. Emerson's poll found that 66.4% of young voters were "very excited to vote," but that also fell below the whole population, where 71% of voters said they were very excited.

Young voter turnout is historically lower than older populations. Della Volpe said that as Gen Zers − who were born between 1997 and 2012− reached voting age in the 2018 and 2022 midterms, strides in participation were made, with the rate of young people voting reaching a record-high 36% in the 2018 midterms, as opposed to a historically typical rate of just 15% to 20%. However, Della Volpe said there is "still a gap" compared to all eligible voters participating at rates between 52% and 54% in 2018 and 2022.

"It would be a lot to expect that young people are going to catch up to older voters in one election cycle," Medina noted. He said when CIRCLE surveyed young voters in February, 55% said they would vote in November. But since survey respondents tend to overestimate their odds of voting, "that doesn't necessarily mean that youth turnout is going to be 55%, which would be beyond historic for a midterm."

news.title: Can House Democrats stay unified next year? It may be up to one man
news.text:
WASHINGTON – For much of this year, infighting among Republicans in the House of Representatives dogged Speaker Mike Johnson, paralyzing his legislative agenda and giving outsized power to singular lawmakers.

On the verge of winning back power, Democrats who slammed the dysfunction may now be facing the same kinds of problems.

If the party takes control of the lower chamber in the midterm elections, as is increasingly expected, the Democratic caucus could include a half-dozen or more far-left lawmakers who took on and defeated incumbents, as well as electorally vulnerable moderates — resulting in clashing agendas and priorities.

At the center of those competing ideologies is Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a Brooklyn-based congressman and the presumptive next speaker of the House.

And at stake is the party’s ability to push back on President Donald Trump during his final two years in office — as well as the brand of the Democratic Party heading into the 2028 presidential election.

“I'm convinced that every single part of the House Democratic caucus will understand the mission, which is deliver for the American people,” Jeffries told USA TODAY in an exclusive interview. “What’s most important, in terms of how I proceed, is us figuring out what unites us.”

Building a 'big tent'

Jeffries, who succeeded former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi as party boss in 2022, told USA TODAY that he believes his party is on the edge of claiming a broad majority that will surpass the exceedingly narrow, two-vote margin that congressional Republicans have been contending with.

“I think we're heading for a more robust majority than that,” Jeffries said. “The goal initially, of course, we’ve got to get to 218, and then we try and win as many seats on top of that as possible.”

A bigger majority would help prevent just two or three members from being able to freeze the House floor for days at a time, though it wouldn't paper over the sometimes bitter disputes over Israel, privacy and other major issues that Democrats will face.

A month before the midterms, Jeffries is gearing up to welcome more progressives, center-left lawmakers and fiscally conservative, moderates to his caucus, rounding out what Democrats have been referring to as their “big tent.” The group is likely to include a handful of self-proclaimed democratic socialists or closely-aligned candidates that ousted allies for whom he had campaigned.

The potential makeup of the caucus has fueled nascent worries among some Democrats about intraparty divisions dragging down their ability to pass bills next year.

"I would hope that we would stick together," Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride told USA TODAY, "whether in the minority or majority.”

A mutiny by moderate members just before the congressional recess cast doubt on whether a new crop of party leaders that includes Jeffries, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark, and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, will be as effective at quelling defiance as the old guard. 

“He's going to have this new flock of DSA candidates and other candidates that are not going to be 100% aligned with his agenda, that are going to have their own objectives, in many cases, to come in and be a disruption,” said Ashley Etienne, who was a senior adviser to Pelosi when the California Democrat when she was House speaker.

As House Democratic leader, Pelosi famously ruled the caucus with an iron fist. But her tenure was not without its publicized skirmishes. She routinely tussled with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who unseated the number four Democrat in the caucus, and other members of the far-left “Squad.”

Warning signs

A month ago, a political wake-up call came for Jeffries and the rest of the House Democratic caucus. Two moderate Blue Dogs, Washington Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and retiring Maine Rep. Jared Golden, crossed party lines to salvage Republicans’ legislative agenda at a critical moment. 

The defiance incensed their colleagues. Jeffries and his chief deputy, Clark, called for a “serious response” to what they characterized as “significant breach of trust.” They’ve since sent mixed messages about how, or whether, they will punish the pair — who’ve teamed up to buck leadership more than once.

Read more: How a bill about whales turned into a warning sign for Democrats

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a former leader of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said party leadership has, in her view, a bad habit of moving “toward the most conservative members.”

"There needs to be some way to make sure that people are part of a team,” the Washington Democrat told USA TODAY, adding: "Nancy had a lot of ways of exercising power.”

Some lawmakers called on Jeffries to strip Gluesenkamp Perez of her sole panel assignment on the powerful Appropriations Committee. Jeffries’ number two, Clark, endorsed a hardline approach, saying Democrats need “team players.” Jayapal also said he “has a right to do that.”

Jeffries declined in the interview with USA TODAY to explain what his response would entail. He did, however, promise a “family conversation” after the midterms – aimed at making sure “we're all operating as a team.”

One party lawmaker, who requested anonymity to speak freely about the dynamics of the caucus, said it would be unwise for Jeffries to crack down before he becomes speaker. The move could alienate lawmakers whose votes he needs to win the job, the lawmaker said.

But former Pelosi adviser and senior White House official Etienne argued that the consequences should have been immediate. 

“It's not just your foes, but your friends are also watching,” Etienne, who worked for Barack Obama and Kamala Harris, said. “Everyone's taking notes in these moments.” 

A new left flank

Unreliable moderates may not be Jeffries' biggest problem in the next Congress, depending on the size of Democrats’ majority. According to Ballotpedia, 23 Democrats announced their retirement or opted to run for other offices. In seven other districts, lawmakers who unseated incumbent Democrats are on the ballot in November, a USA TODAY analysis shows.

“It's important to recognize that the blue wave is likely to be a progressive wave,” said Joseph Geevarghese, the executive director of the progressive activist group Our Revolution. “And the incoming class of progressives has clear demands.”

Several of those anti-establishment candidates have refused to say if they’ll back Jeffries for speaker, setting up a potential clash with party leadership from the get-go. They include Melat Kiros in Colorado, Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York and Adam Hamawy in New Jersey.

Jeffries told USA TODAY he’s had conversations with every single candidate “who's won the Democratic nomination and is on their way into serving in the next Congress,” including those in New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia, Denver and Detroit, “who may fall into that category.”

In an interview, Rep. Ro Khanna, a progressive Democrat from California, also said he’d help Jeffries whip votes.

Geevarghese said incoming lawmakers need to be strategic about when and how to confront leadership. He held up the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ approach during former President Joe Biden’s presidency, when the Democrat was pushing his Build Back Better agenda through Congress, as an example of how to extract concessions from the establishment.

The progressive activist advised new members to work through the existing group to force votes on policy priorities like Medicaid for All in the next legislative session.

“It’s incumbent that the caucus acts together and is disciplined in support of that policy and other progressive policies that get advanced and not acting as lone wolves,” Geevarghese said.

news.text:

news.title: Karine Jean-Pierre says Trump is making same mistake as Biden on fulfilling his agenda
news.text:
Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre argued in an opinion piece published Friday that President Donald Trump was making the same messaging mistakes as her former boss, former President Joe Biden.

“Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda,” she wrote in The New York Times guest essay. “His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land. 

“Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation.”

Jean-Pierre pointed to the president’s messaging on gas prices, inflation and the war in Iran in the piece and said, “When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses.”

“The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging,” she wrote.

When asked about Jean-Pierre’s argument, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital in a statement, “Biden’s policies destroyed our economy by creating the worst inflation crisis in history, instituting burdensome red tape and stifling American energy dominance. 

“President Trump has fixed the disaster that Joe Biden created by cooling inflation, signing the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, lowering drug prices and reshoring our manufacturing industry. The fake news won’t, so President Trump will continue to tout his economic wins to Americans.”

Jean-Pierre admitted the Biden administration misread the public and said her press briefings fueled much of the debate surrounding Biden’s age, in addition to the economic messaging.

“We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it,” she conceded.

She also pointed to the changing media ecosystem and said a “TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump” would get more attention than her press briefings or a Cabinet official on the Sunday news programs.

“The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds,” Jean-Pierre wrote. 

“His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated.

“Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now.”

Jean-Pierre released a book in 2025, “Independent,” about her time in the White House. 

Ahead of its release, she revealed she was leaving the Democratic Party and registering as an Independent.

“The Democratic Party had defined my life, my career,” Jean-Pierre wrote. 

“Everything I’d done to make people’s lives better had been connected to it. The party was the vehicle that allowed me not just to have a front seat to history, working first on [Barack] Obama’s presidential campaign then in his administration, but also to make some history of my own as the first Black woman and openly queer person to ever be a White House press secretary. Never had I considered leaving the party until now.”
news.summary: In a New York Times essay, Karine Jean-Pierre warns that Donald Trump is repeating Joe Biden's mistake of ignoring voters' lived economic realities.
